title: AP Physics 1
description: Free AP Physics 1 study guide: 8 units, 320 practice questions, 80 flashcards, quick reference, memory tricks, and a full practice exam. Completely free.

units.name: Kinematics

concepts.intro: Position locates an object relative to an origin; displacement is the vector change in position, while distance is the scalar path length traveled.
b: Displacement Δx = x_f − x_i (vector, can be negative)
Distance is always positive and ≥ |displacement|
Displacement depends only on start/end points, not the path
On a position-vs-time graph, slope = velocity
Average velocity = Δx/Δt; average speed = total distance/total time

concepts.intro: Velocity is the rate of change of position; acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
b: Instantaneous velocity = slope of the tangent line on an x-t graph
Acceleration a = Δv/Δt, units m/s²
On a v-t graph, slope = acceleration and area under the curve = displacement
Object speeds up when v and a have the same sign; slows down when opposite signs
Constant velocity means zero acceleration (straight line on x-t graph)

concepts.intro: For motion with constant acceleration, four kinematic equations relate displacement, velocity, acceleration, and time.
b: v = v₀ + at
Δx = v₀t + ½at²
v² = v₀² + 2aΔx
Δx = ½(v₀ + v)t
Choose the equation missing the variable you don't know or don't need
These equations only apply when acceleration is constant

concepts.intro: Free fall is motion under gravity alone (a = −9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface); projectile motion combines horizontal (constant velocity) and vertical (constant acceleration) motion independently.
b: g = 9.8 m/s² downward, same for all objects (ignoring air resistance)
Horizontal velocity stays constant (a_x = 0) during projectile motion
Vertical motion uses the kinematic equations with a = −g
Time to reach max height: t = v_y0/g; at max height v_y = 0
Range R = (v₀² sin2θ)/g for equal launch/landing height
Horizontal and vertical motions are independent but share the same time variable

concepts.intro: Position, velocity, and acceleration graphs are linked through slope and area relationships.
b: Slope of x-t graph = velocity; slope of v-t graph = acceleration
Area under v-t graph = displacement; area under a-t graph = Δv
A parabolic x-t graph indicates constant nonzero acceleration
A horizontal line on a v-t graph means constant velocity (zero acceleration)
Curvature direction on x-t graph shows whether acceleration is positive or negative

concepts.intro: Vector quantities in kinematics (displacement, velocity, acceleration) must be added using vector addition, and can be decomposed into perpendicular components.
b: Vector components: vₓ = v cosθ, v_y = v sinθ
Magnitude from components: v = √(vₓ² + v_y²)
Relative velocity: v_AC = v_AB + v_BC (vector addition)
Independent x and y motions can be analyzed separately then recombined
Angle of resultant: θ = tan⁻¹(v_y/vₓ)

keyFacts: v = v₀ + at, Δx = v₀t + ½at², v² = v₀² + 2aΔx, Δx = ½(v₀+v)t
g = 9.8 m/s² (downward) near Earth's surface for all free-falling objects
Slope of x-t graph = velocity; slope of v-t graph = acceleration; area under v-t graph = displacement
Projectile motion: horizontal velocity constant, vertical acceleration = −g, time is shared between axes
traps: Velocity and acceleration can point in different directions (deceleration is negative-signed a relative to v, not always 'negative a'), not 'acceleration always means speeding up'
At the top of a projectile's path, vertical velocity is zero but vertical acceleration is still −g, not zero
Distance traveled equals |displacement| only for one-directional motion, not always equal in general
A steeper x-t graph means greater speed, not greater position; curvature (not steepness alone) indicates acceleration

units.name: Dynamics & Newton's Laws

concepts.intro: An object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force.
b: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist changes in its motion
Mass is the quantitative measure of inertia
Net force = 0 means constant velocity (including rest), not necessarily no motion
This law defines an inertial reference frame
Equilibrium (ΣF=0) applies to both static and moving-at-constant-velocity objects

concepts.intro: The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration, and acceleration is in the direction of the net force.
b: ΣF = ma, where ΣF is the vector sum of all forces
Acceleration is directly proportional to net force, inversely proportional to mass
Must use net (unbalanced) force, not any single applied force
Free-body diagrams isolate all forces acting on one object
Apply F=ma separately along perpendicular axes (e.g., x and y) when forces are 2D

concepts.intro: For every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force acting on a different object.
b: Action-reaction pairs act on two different objects, so they never cancel for a single object
Pairs are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, same type of force
Normal force from a table on a book pairs with the book pushing down on the table
Third law pairs act simultaneously, not one after another
Used to analyze contact forces, tension, and collisions

concepts.l: Common Forces: Weight, Normal, Tension, Friction
concepts.intro: Several named forces recur throughout dynamics problems and each has a specific formula and direction.
b: Weight Fg = mg, always points toward Earth's center
Normal force N is perpendicular to the contact surface, adjusts to prevent penetration
Tension is a pulling force transmitted through a string/rope, same throughout an ideal (massless, frictionless-pulley) string
Static friction f_s ≤ μ_s N (prevents motion); kinetic friction f_k = μ_k N (opposes sliding motion)
μ_k is generally less than or equal to μ_s for the same surfaces

concepts.intro: On an incline, gravity is decomposed into components parallel and perpendicular to the surface; connected objects (via strings/pulleys) share acceleration magnitude.
b: Component of gravity along incline: mg sinθ; perpendicular: mg cosθ
Normal force on a frictionless incline: N = mg cosθ
For connected masses over a pulley, treat the system together (a is the same magnitude for both) or use separate free-body diagrams
Tension is generally not equal to the weight of a hanging accelerating mass
Draw a separate free-body diagram for each object in multi-body problems

concepts.intro: Apparent weight (the normal force felt) differs from true weight when an object accelerates vertically, as in an elevator.
b: Apparent weight N = m(g + a) when accelerating upward
Apparent weight N = m(g − a) when accelerating downward
In free fall (a = g downward), apparent weight is zero (weightlessness)
Constant velocity elevator: apparent weight = true weight (a=0)
Scale readings measure normal force, not gravitational force directly

keyFacts: ΣF = ma (Newton's Second Law) — net force determines acceleration
Newton's Third Law pairs act on different objects, equal magnitude, opposite direction
f_s(max) = μ_s N, f_k = μ_k N — friction is proportional to the normal force
On a frictionless incline: a = g sinθ; N = mg cosθ
traps: A moving object needs a net force only to change its velocity, not to keep moving at constant velocity ('no force needed to sustain motion' is correct, not 'motion requires continuous force')
Action-reaction pairs act on two different objects and never cancel each other for a single free-body diagram, not 'forces on the same object cancel'
Normal force is not always equal to mg — it depends on other forces and acceleration (e.g., on an incline or in an elevator), not a fixed value
Static friction is a variable up to a maximum (μ_s N), not always exactly μ_s N

units.name: Energy & Work

concepts.intro: Work is the transfer of energy via a force acting through a displacement, and depends on the angle between force and displacement.
b: W = Fd cosθ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement
Work is zero if force is perpendicular to displacement (θ=90°)
Work is positive when force has a component in the direction of motion, negative when opposite
Units of work are joules (J) = N·m
Work-energy theorem: net work done equals the change in kinetic energy, W_net = ΔKE

concepts.intro: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion, and the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.
b: KE = ½mv²
W_net = ΔKE = KE_f − KE_i
Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so doubling speed quadruples KE
The work-energy theorem applies regardless of the path taken
Only the net (total) work changes kinetic energy; individual forces can do positive or negative work

concepts.intro: Potential energy is stored energy associated with an object's position or configuration, recoverable as kinetic energy.
b: Gravitational PE: U_g = mgh, measured relative to a chosen reference height
Elastic (spring) PE: U_s = ½kx², where x is displacement from equilibrium
PE depends on relative position, so only changes in PE are physically meaningful
Conservative forces (gravity, spring) have path-independent work
Hooke's Law: F_spring = −kx describes the restoring force of an ideal spring

concepts.intro: In the absence of non-conservative forces (like friction), total mechanical energy (KE + PE) remains constant.
b: KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f (when no friction/air resistance)
With friction: KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f + energy lost to heat (ΔE_thermal)
Energy 'lost' to friction equals the work done by friction (magnitude), W_friction = f·d
Roller coasters, pendulums, and sliding blocks are classic conservation-of-energy scenarios
Total energy of an isolated system is always conserved, even when mechanical energy is not

concepts.intro: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.
b: P = W/t = ΔE/t, units are watts (W) = J/s
Instantaneous power: P = Fv cosθ (force times velocity component along force direction)
Average power over a time interval uses total work divided by total time
Higher power means doing the same work in less time, not necessarily more work
1 horsepower ≈ 746 W (useful for real-world comparisons)

concepts.intro: Energy bar charts and system diagrams track how energy transforms and transfers between kinetic, potential, and thermal forms.
b: A closed/isolated system conserves total energy; energy only transforms between forms
Energy bar charts show relative amounts of KE, PE, and thermal energy at different points
Non-conservative forces (friction, applied pushes) change total mechanical energy of a system
Choosing the system boundary determines whether work is 'external' or energy transformation is 'internal'
Elastic collisions conserve KE; inelastic collisions convert some KE to other forms (heat, sound, deformation)

keyFacts: W = Fd cosθ; W_net = ΔKE (work-energy theorem)
KE = ½mv²; U_g = mgh; U_spring = ½kx²
Conservation of mechanical energy (no friction): KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f
Power P = W/t = Fv cosθ; units are watts (J/s)
traps: Work done by a force perpendicular to displacement is zero, not simply 'less work' — cosθ=0 makes it exactly zero (e.g., normal force does no work on a moving object)
Potential energy is only meaningful as a difference/change (ΔPE), not an absolute value — the reference point is arbitrary
Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so doubling velocity quadruples KE, not just doubles it
Friction converts mechanical energy to thermal energy (it doesn't destroy energy) — total energy is still conserved, only mechanical energy decreases

units.name: Momentum

concepts.intro: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity, and impulse is the change in momentum caused by a force acting over time.
b: p = mv, a vector quantity in the direction of velocity
Impulse J = FΔt = Δp (impulse-momentum theorem)
Impulse equals the area under a force-vs-time graph
A larger Δt for the same Δp reduces the average force needed (e.g., airbags, padding)
Units of momentum: kg·m/s; units of impulse: N·s (equivalent)

concepts.intro: In an isolated system (no external net force), total momentum before an interaction equals total momentum after.
b: p_total,initial = p_total,final for an isolated system
Momentum is conserved in all collision types (elastic, inelastic, perfectly inelastic) as long as the system is isolated
Must account for direction—momentum is a vector, so opposite-direction velocities subtract
External forces (like friction or gravity) can change total system momentum unless balanced or negligible over the interaction time
For explosions, initial total momentum (often zero) equals the vector sum of final momenta of the fragments

concepts.intro: Collisions are classified by whether kinetic energy is conserved in addition to momentum.
b: Elastic collision: both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
Inelastic collision: momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is not (some converts to heat/sound/deformation)
Perfectly inelastic collision: objects stick together and move with a common final velocity
Real-world macroscopic collisions are usually inelastic to some degree
For a perfectly inelastic collision: m1v1+m2v2=(m1+m2)v_f

concepts.intro: Collision problems use conservation of momentum (always) and conservation of kinetic energy (only if elastic) as simultaneous equations.
b: Set up conservation of momentum: Σp_before = Σp_after
For elastic collisions, also apply KE_before = KE_after as a second equation
Choose a positive direction convention and keep velocity signs consistent
1D collisions: use scalar (signed) velocities; 2D collisions require resolving momentum by x and y components separately
Check the answer's physical reasonableness (e.g., objects shouldn't pass through each other)

concepts.intro: The center of mass is the weighted average position of a system's mass, and it moves according to the net external force on the whole system.
b: The center of mass of an isolated system moves at constant velocity, even if individual parts collide or explode
Internal forces (like collision forces or explosions) do not change the center of mass motion
In projectile explosions, the center of mass continues along the original trajectory as if no explosion occurred
For symmetric objects, the center of mass is at the geometric center

concepts.intro: Momentum conservation extends to two dimensions by conserving x- and y-components independently, applicable to collisions, sports, and vehicle safety design.
b: Conserve momentum separately along perpendicular axes: Σp_x,before=Σp_x,after and Σp_y,before=Σp_y,after
Glancing collisions require vector decomposition of initial and final velocities
Crumple zones in cars increase collision time Δt, reducing force for a given impulse (Δp)
Rocket propulsion relies on momentum conservation between expelled fuel and the rocket
Recoil (e.g., a gun firing) is explained by conservation of momentum: the gun's backward momentum matches the bullet's forward momentum

keyFacts: p = mv; Impulse J = FΔt = Δp
Momentum is conserved in isolated systems: Σp_before = Σp_after
Elastic collisions conserve both momentum and KE; inelastic collisions conserve only momentum
Perfectly inelastic collision: m1v1 + m2v2 = (m1+m2)v_f
traps: Kinetic energy is generally NOT conserved in real-world (inelastic) collisions, even though momentum always is, not 'both are always conserved together'
Momentum is a vector — velocities in opposite directions must be given opposite signs, not treated as simply additive magnitudes
A larger force isn't needed for a bigger impulse if time increases proportionally — impulse depends on both F and Δt, not force alone
The center of mass of a system continues on its original path during an internal explosion or collision (external force unchanged), not 'the pieces ignore the original motion'

units.name: Circular Motion & Gravity

concepts.intro: An object moving in a circle at constant speed still accelerates because its velocity direction constantly changes; this acceleration points toward the center of the circle.
b: Centripetal acceleration a_c = v²/r = ω²r, always directed toward the center
Period T = 2πr/v = 2π/ω; frequency f = 1/T
Speed is constant in uniform circular motion, but velocity is not (direction changes)
Angular velocity ω = v/r, units rad/s
Centripetal acceleration exists even though speed doesn't change — it's caused by the change in direction
Tangential acceleration (if speed changes) is separate from centripetal acceleration and points along the path

concepts.intro: Centripetal force is not a new type of force but the net force directed toward the center that causes circular motion; it must be supplied by real forces (tension, gravity, friction, normal force).
b: F_c = mv²/r = mω²r, always points toward the center of the circular path
F_c is the net force in the radial direction, not a separate force added to a free-body diagram
Examples: tension supplies F_c for a ball on a string; gravity supplies F_c for orbiting satellites; static friction supplies F_c for a car turning on a flat road
On a banked curve, a component of the normal force contributes to centripetal force
If the centripetal force vanishes, the object moves off in a straight line (tangent to the circle), not outward radially
Maximum speed on a flat curve before slipping: v_max = √(μ_s g r)

concepts.intro: When circular motion occurs in a vertical plane, gravity adds to or subtracts from the required centripetal force depending on position in the loop.
b: At the top of a vertical loop: F_c = N + mg (both point toward center, downward)
At the bottom of a vertical loop: F_c = N − mg (N points up toward center, mg points away)
Minimum speed at the top of a loop (N = 0): v_min = √(gr)
Apparent weight is greatest at the bottom of a loop and least at the top
A roller coaster or pendulum at the top of its arc still needs centripetal force directed downward, toward the center

concepts.intro: Every pair of masses attracts each other with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers.
b: F_g = Gm₁m₂/r², where G = 6.674×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²
r is measured between the centers of mass, not the surfaces
Gravitational force is always attractive and acts along the line joining the two masses
Doubling the distance reduces the force to 1/4 (inverse-square law)
Gravitational field strength g = GM/r², which is why g decreases with altitude
Newton's third law applies: the force on mass 1 from mass 2 equals in magnitude the force on mass 2 from mass 1

concepts.intro: A satellite or planet in a stable circular orbit has gravity acting as the sole centripetal force, which links orbital speed and period to the orbit's radius.
b: Setting gravity equal to centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r gives orbital speed v = √(GM/r)
Orbital period: T = 2πr/v = 2π√(r³/GM)
Orbital speed and period depend only on the central mass M and orbital radius r, not on the orbiting object's mass
A larger orbital radius means a slower orbital speed and a longer period
Geostationary satellites orbit with T = 24 hours, matching Earth's rotation

concepts.intro: Kepler's laws describe planetary orbits, and gravitational potential energy (defined as zero at infinite separation) is always negative for a bound system.
b: Kepler's First Law: planets orbit the Sun in ellipses with the Sun at one focus
Kepler's Second Law: a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times (faster when closer to the Sun)
Kepler's Third Law: T² ∝ r³ for objects orbiting the same central body
Gravitational PE: U_g = −GMm/r (negative, approaching zero as r→∞)
Escape velocity: v_esc = √(2GM/r), the minimum speed to escape a gravitational field from radius r
Total mechanical energy of a bound orbit (KE + U_g) is negative; unbound trajectories have E ≥ 0

keyFacts: a_c = v²/r = ω²r (always toward center); F_c = mv²/r is the net radial force, not an extra force
F_g = Gm₁m₂/r², G = 6.674×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²
Orbital speed v = √(GM/r); orbital period T = 2π√(r³/GM); Kepler's Third Law: T² ∝ r³
Minimum speed at top of vertical loop: v_min = √(gr); gravitational PE: U_g = −GMm/r
traps: Centripetal force is the net inward force supplied by real forces (tension, gravity, friction, normal), not a separate force you add to a free-body diagram
If centripetal force disappears, an object flies off tangent to the circle (in a straight line), not radially outward
Orbital speed and period depend only on the central mass and orbital radius, not on the orbiting satellite's own mass
Doubling the orbital radius does NOT halve the orbital speed — v ∝ 1/√r, so speed decreases by a factor of √2

units.name: Rotational Motion

concepts.intro: Rotational motion uses angular analogues of the linear kinematic quantities and equations, connected to linear quantities through the radius.
b: Angular position θ (rad), angular velocity ω = Δθ/Δt, angular acceleration α = Δω/Δt
Linear-angular relationships: v = ωr, a_tangential = αr, a_centripetal = ω²r
Rotational kinematic equations (constant α): ω = ω₀ + αt; Δθ = ω₀t + ½αt²; ω² = ω₀² + 2αΔθ
One full revolution = 2π radians = 360°
These equations are structurally identical to the linear kinematics equations with x→θ, v→ω, a→α

concepts.intro: Torque is the rotational analogue of force — it measures how effectively a force causes angular acceleration about a pivot, depending on both the force and where/how it's applied.
b: τ = rF sinθ, where θ is the angle between the position vector (from pivot to force) and the force
τ = rF⊥, using only the component of force perpendicular to the lever arm (r)
Torque is maximized when force is applied perpendicular to the lever arm (θ = 90°) and zero when force is applied along the lever arm (θ = 0°)
Units of torque: N·m (not joules, even though the units are dimensionally the same)
Sign convention: counterclockwise torque is typically positive, clockwise is negative
Net torque causes angular acceleration: Στ = Iα

concepts.intro: Moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass — it measures an object's resistance to changes in angular velocity, depending on both mass and how that mass is distributed relative to the axis.
b: I = Σm_ir_i² for point masses; distributed mass is found by integration or standard formulas
Common formulas: solid sphere I = ₅⁄₂MR², solid disk/cylinder I = ½MR², hoop/ring I = MR², rod about center I = ¹⁄₁₂ML², rod about end I = ₁⁄₃ML²
Mass farther from the axis contributes more to I (I depends on r², not just mass)
The same object has a different I depending on the chosen rotation axis
Parallel axis theorem: I = I_cm + Md², where d is the distance from the center-of-mass axis to the new axis

concepts.intro: Newton's second law has a rotational form relating net torque to angular acceleration, and static equilibrium requires both zero net force and zero net torque.
b: Στ = Iα (rotational analogue of ΣF = ma)
For static equilibrium: ΣF = 0 AND Στ = 0 (about any chosen pivot point)
Choosing the pivot at the location of an unknown force eliminates that force from the torque equation
Rolling without slipping requires v_cm = ωr and a_cm = αr
An object can have zero net force but nonzero net torque (it accelerates angularly while its center of mass doesn't accelerate linearly), and vice versa

concepts.intro: Angular momentum is the rotational analogue of linear momentum, and it is conserved for a system when there is no net external torque.
b: L = Iω for a rotating rigid body; L = mvr sinθ for a point particle about an axis
Conservation of angular momentum: L_initial = L_final when Στ_ext = 0
If moment of inertia decreases (mass pulled closer to axis), angular velocity must increase to conserve L (e.g., spinning ice skater pulling in arms)
Angular impulse: τΔt = ΔL (rotational analogue of J = FΔt = Δp)
Angular momentum is conserved even when kinetic energy is not (e.g., an inelastic rotational collision)

concepts.intro: A rotating object stores kinetic energy in its rotation, and a rolling object has both translational and rotational kinetic energy.
b: Rotational KE = ½Iω²
Total KE of a rolling object: KE_total = ½Mv_cm² + ½Iω²
For rolling without slipping, use v_cm = ωr to combine the two KE terms
An object with a larger moment of inertia (for the same mass/radius) rolls down an incline more slowly because more energy goes into rotation
Energy conservation for rolling down a hill: mgh = ½mv² + ½Iω² (no energy lost if rolling without slipping, since static friction does no work)

keyFacts: τ = rF sinθ; Στ = Iα (rotational analogue of ΣF = ma)
I = Σmr² (point masses); common shapes: disk ½MR², hoop MR², sphere ₅⁄₂MR², rod about center ¹⁄₁₂ML²
L = Iω, conserved when net external torque is zero
Rotational KE = ½Iω²; rolling object KE = ½Mv² + ½Iω² (using v = ωr)
traps: Torque depends on where a force is applied and its angle to the lever arm, not just its magnitude — a large force applied along the lever arm produces zero torque
Moment of inertia depends on the axis of rotation, not just the object's mass — the same object has different I values about different axes
Angular momentum conservation applies even when kinetic energy is not conserved, not 'both are always conserved together'
Rolling without slipping requires v_cm = ωr; a sliding (skidding) object does not satisfy this relationship

units.name: Waves & Sound

concepts.intro: Waves transfer energy without net transfer of matter, and their properties are related through a single equation connecting speed, wavelength, and frequency.
b: Wave speed v = fλ, where f is frequency (Hz) and λ is wavelength (m)
Period T = 1/f is the time for one complete cycle
Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium and determines the wave's energy (intensity ∝ amplitude²)
Transverse waves (e.g., light, waves on a string) oscillate perpendicular to the direction of travel; longitudinal waves (e.g., sound) oscillate parallel to it
Wave speed on a string depends on tension and linear mass density: v = √(F_T/μ), not on frequency or amplitude
Frequency is set by the source and does not change when a wave passes into a new medium; wavelength and speed do change

concepts.intro: When two or more waves overlap in the same medium, their displacements add algebraically (superposition), producing constructive or destructive interference.
b: Principle of superposition: net displacement = sum of individual wave displacements at that point
Constructive interference occurs when waves are in phase (crest meets crest), producing a larger amplitude
Destructive interference occurs when waves are out of phase (crest meets trough), reducing or canceling amplitude
Path difference of a whole number of wavelengths (nλ) gives constructive interference; a half-integer number ((n+½)λ) gives destructive interference
After waves pass through each other, they continue unaffected (superposition is temporary, not permanent)
Beats occur when two waves of slightly different frequencies interfere, producing a periodic amplitude variation with beat frequency f_beat = |f₁ − f₂|

concepts.intro: Standing waves form when two identical waves traveling in opposite directions interfere, creating fixed points of no displacement (nodes) and maximum displacement (antinodes).
b: Nodes are points of zero displacement; antinodes are points of maximum displacement, spaced λ/2 apart
String fixed at both ends: λ_n = 2L/n, f_n = nv/(2L) for n = 1, 2, 3,… (harmonics)
Pipe open at both ends: same harmonic series as a string, λ_n = 2L/n
Pipe closed at one end: only odd harmonics, λ_n = 4L/n for n = 1, 3, 5,…
Resonance occurs when a driving frequency matches a system's natural frequency, producing a large-amplitude standing wave
The fundamental frequency (n=1) is the lowest possible resonant frequency for a given system

concepts.intro: Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave that requires a medium to travel, with speed depending on the properties of that medium.
b: Sound speed in air at room temperature ≈ 343 m/s; sound travels faster in solids and liquids than in gases
Sound intensity (power per area) decreases with distance following an inverse-square law: I ∝ 1/r²
Sound level in decibels: β = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀), where I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m² is the threshold of hearing
Pitch corresponds to frequency; loudness corresponds to amplitude/intensity
Sound cannot travel through a vacuum because it requires a medium to propagate

concepts.intro: The Doppler effect is the change in observed frequency of a wave when there is relative motion between the source and the observer.
b: Frequency increases when the source and observer are moving toward each other, decreases when moving apart
General formula: f_observed = f_source × (v ± v_observer)/(v ∓ v_source), using + for approach and − for recession in each term
Only relative motion along the line connecting source and observer matters
The Doppler effect changes the observed frequency (and wavelength), not the actual speed of the wave in the medium
Applications: radar guns, redshift/blueshift of light from stars, weather Doppler radar

concepts.intro: When a wave reaches a boundary between media, part of it reflects and part transmits, with the details depending on the relative properties of the two media.
b: A wave reflecting off a fixed (denser medium) boundary inverts (180° phase shift)
A wave reflecting off a free (less dense medium) boundary reflects without inversion
Refraction occurs when a wave changes speed crossing into a new medium, which can bend its direction of travel
Diffraction is the bending/spreading of waves around obstacles or through openings, more pronounced when the opening size is comparable to the wavelength
Total wave energy is split between reflected and transmitted waves at a boundary

keyFacts: v = fλ; wave speed on a string v = √(F_T/μ); frequency is set by the source and unchanged across media
String fixed at both ends / open-open pipe: f_n = nv/(2L); closed-open pipe: f_n = nv/(4L), odd n only
Doppler effect: f_observed = f_source(v ± v_obs)/(v ∓ v_src); approach raises frequency, recession lowers it
Constructive interference: path difference = nλ; destructive interference: path difference = (n+½)λ
traps: Wave frequency is determined by the source and stays the same when a wave enters a new medium — wavelength and speed change, not frequency
A closed-open pipe only supports odd harmonics (f_n = nv/4L, n=1,3,5...), unlike an open-open pipe or a string, which supports all integer harmonics
The Doppler effect changes the observed frequency, not the actual wave speed through the medium
Sound cannot travel through a vacuum because it is a mechanical (longitudinal) wave requiring a medium, unlike light

units.name: Electrostatics & Circuits

concepts.intro: Electric charge is a fundamental property of matter that comes in two types (positive and negative), and Coulomb's law describes the force between two point charges.
b: Coulomb's Law: F = kq₁q₂/r², where k = 8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C²
Like charges repel; opposite charges attract, with the force acting along the line joining them
Charge is quantized in units of e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C and is conserved in any closed system
Coulomb's law has the same inverse-square form as gravity, but can be attractive or repulsive (gravity is only attractive)
Conductors allow charge to move freely; insulators do not
Charging by induction separates charge without direct contact; charging by friction/contact transfers charge directly

concepts.intro: An electric field is the region around a charge where another charge would feel a force, defined as force per unit charge.
b: E = F/q = kQ/r² (field due to a point charge Q), units N/C
Electric field lines point away from positive charges and toward negative charges
Field line density represents field strength; field lines never cross
Force on a charge in a field: F = qE, in the direction of E for positive q, opposite for negative q
A uniform field (e.g., between parallel plates) has evenly spaced, parallel field lines
Superposition applies to electric fields: the net field is the vector sum of fields from all sources

concepts.intro: Electric potential energy is the energy stored due to the position of a charge in a field, and electric potential is potential energy per unit charge.
b: Electric potential V = U/q, units volts (V) = J/C
Potential difference (voltage) drives current: ΔV = W/q, the work done per unit charge moving between two points
For a uniform field: E = ΔV/d, relating field strength to voltage across a distance d
Positive charges move from high to low potential naturally (like a ball rolling downhill); electrons move from low to high potential
Equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to electric field lines, and no work is done moving a charge along one

concepts.intro: Electric current is the rate of charge flow through a conductor, and Ohm's law relates voltage, current, and resistance for many materials.
b: Current I = ΔQ/Δt, units amperes (A) = C/s
Ohm's Law: V = IR, where R is resistance in ohms (Ω)
Resistance of a wire: R = ρL/A, increasing with length and resistivity, decreasing with cross-sectional area
Conventional current flows from + to − externally (opposite to actual electron flow)
Electric power: P = IV = I²R = V²/R
Resistivity ρ generally increases with temperature for metals (more collisions impede electron flow)

concepts.intro: Resistors combine differently depending on whether they are connected in series (single path) or parallel (multiple paths), affecting current, voltage, and equivalent resistance.
b: Series: same current through each resistor; R_eq = R₁ + R₂ + ...; voltages add (V_total = V₁ + V₂ + ...)
Parallel: same voltage across each resistor; 1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ...; currents add (I_total = I₁ + I₂ + ...)
Adding a resistor in series always increases total resistance; adding a resistor in parallel always decreases total resistance
Equivalent resistance of parallel resistors is always less than the smallest individual resistance
Ammeters are connected in series (low resistance); voltmeters are connected in parallel (high resistance)

concepts.intro: Kirchhoff's rules formalize conservation of charge and energy in circuits, allowing analysis of complex multi-loop networks.
b: Kirchhoff's Junction Rule: total current into a junction equals total current out (conservation of charge)
Kirchhoff's Loop Rule: the sum of voltage changes around any closed loop equals zero (conservation of energy)
Real batteries have internal resistance r, so terminal voltage V = EMF − Ir (less than EMF when current flows)
Power delivered by a source: P = I × EMF; power dissipated in a resistor: P = I²R
For circuits with both series and parallel sections, simplify parallel branches to an equivalent resistor first, then combine in series

keyFacts: Coulomb's Law: F = kq₁q₂/r², k = 8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C²; E = F/q = kQ/r²
Ohm's Law: V = IR; Power P = IV = I²R = V²/R
Series: R_eq = R₁+R₂+...; same I. Parallel: 1/R_eq = 1/R₁+1/R₂+...; same V
Kirchhoff's rules: ΣI_in = ΣI_out (junction); ΣΔV = 0 around a closed loop
traps: Adding a resistor in parallel decreases total resistance (creates another path for current), not increases it like adding one in series
Current is the same through every resistor in series, not the voltage — voltage divides; in parallel, voltage is the same and current divides
Equivalent resistance of resistors in parallel is always less than the smallest individual resistor, not an average of the values
Conventional current direction (+ to −) is opposite to the actual direction electrons move, which matters when interpreting circuit diagrams

quiz.q: A 0.50 kg ball moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.80 m at a constant speed of 4.0 m/s. What is the centripetal acceleration?
Using the same ball (m = 0.50 kg, v = 4.0 m/s, r = 0.80 m), what is the centripetal force?
A car of mass 1200 kg rounds a flat curve of radius 50 m at 20 m/s. What minimum coefficient of static friction is needed?
What provides the centripetal force for a satellite in circular orbit around Earth?
quiz.e: Gravity is the only force acting on an orbiting satellite, and it points toward Earth's center, exactly matching the direction needed for centripetal force.

quiz.q: If the centripetal force on an object in circular motion suddenly disappears, the object will:
o: Move in a straight line tangent to the circle
Fly directly outward, away from the center
quiz.e: With no net force, Newton's first law says the object moves in a straight line in the direction of its instantaneous velocity, which is tangent to the circle.

quiz.q: A ball on a string moves in a vertical circle. At the top of the circle, which equation correctly gives the centripetal force?
quiz.e: At the top, both the tension/normal force N and gravity mg point downward, toward the center, so they add: F_c = N + mg.

quiz.q: What is the minimum speed a roller coaster car needs at the top of a vertical loop of radius 9.0 m to maintain contact with the track?
quiz.e: At minimum speed, N = 0, so mg = mv^2/r, giving v = sqrt(gr) = sqrt(9.8 x 9.0) = sqrt(88.2) = 9.4 m/s.

quiz.q: Two point masses are separated by distance r and exert gravitational force F on each other. If the distance is tripled, the new force is:
quiz.e: Gravitational force follows an inverse-square law: F = Gm1m2/r^2. Tripling r reduces F by a factor of 3^2 = 9, so new force = F/9.

quiz.q: Two objects each have their mass doubled while the distance between them stays the same. The gravitational force between them becomes:
quiz.e: F = Gm1m2/r^2. Doubling both masses multiplies the product m1m2 by 4, so the force increases by a factor of 4.

quiz.q: What is the value of the universal gravitational constant G?
quiz.e: G = 6.674 x 10^-11 N*m^2/kg^2 is the universal gravitational constant used in Newton's law of gravitation.

quiz.q: A planet has twice Earth's mass and twice Earth's radius. Compared to Earth's surface gravity g, the planet's surface gravity is:
quiz.e: g = GM/r^2. Doubling M multiplies g by 2; doubling r divides g by 4. Net effect: g x 2/4 = g/2.

quiz.q: A satellite orbits Earth at radius r with orbital speed v. If the orbital radius is increased to 4r, the new orbital speed is:
quiz.e: v = sqrt(GM/r), so v is proportional to 1/sqrt(r). Increasing r by a factor of 4 decreases v by a factor of sqrt(4) = 2, giving v/2.

quiz.q: Kepler's Third Law states that for objects orbiting the same central body:
quiz.e: Kepler's Third Law: T^2 proportional to r^3, derivable by combining Newton's gravitation with centripetal force requirements.

quiz.q: Planet A orbits at radius r with period T. Planet B orbits the same star at radius 4r. What is Planet B's period?
quiz.e: T^2 proportional to r^3. If r increases by 4x, T^2 increases by 4^3 = 64x, so T increases by sqrt(64) = 8x, giving 8T.

quiz.q: Gravitational potential energy between two masses, using U=0 at infinite separation, is given by:
quiz.e: U_g = -GMm/r is negative for any finite separation, approaching zero only as r approaches infinity.

quiz.q: As two masses are moved farther apart (r increases), their gravitational potential energy:
quiz.e: Since U = -GMm/r, increasing r makes the magnitude of U smaller, so U becomes less negative, i.e., increases toward zero.

quiz.q: What is escape velocity from a planet of mass M and radius R?
quiz.e: Escape velocity is found by setting total mechanical energy to zero: (1/2)mv^2 - GMm/R = 0, giving v_esc = sqrt(2GM/R).

quiz.q: A geostationary satellite has an orbital period of:
quiz.e: A geostationary satellite orbits with the same period as Earth's rotation, 24 hours, so it appears stationary above a fixed point on Earth.

quiz.q: A car negotiates a frictionless banked curve of radius r at angle theta. Which expression gives the correct speed for no reliance on friction?
quiz.e: On a frictionless banked curve, the horizontal component of the normal force supplies centripetal force: N sin(theta) = mv^2/r and N cos(theta) = mg, giving tan(theta) = v^2/(rg), so v = sqrt(rg tan(theta)).

quiz.q: A 1000 kg car rounds a banked curve (frictionless) of radius 100 m banked at 20 degrees. What speed keeps it on the path without relying on friction?
quiz.e: v = sqrt(rg tan(theta)) = sqrt(100 x 9.8 x tan(20 deg)) = sqrt(980 x 0.364) = sqrt(356.7) = 18.9 ~ 19 m/s.

quiz.q: Which of the following is constant for a satellite in uniform circular orbit?
o: Acceleration direction relative to Earth's surface below it
Net force direction in space (fixed direction)
quiz.e: In uniform circular motion, speed (magnitude of velocity) stays constant, but velocity direction, and hence the direction of the centripetal acceleration/force in space, continuously changes.

quiz.q: What is the period of a satellite orbiting at radius r around a planet of mass M?
quiz.e: Setting gravity equal to centripetal force and solving for period gives T = 2*pi*sqrt(r^3/GM).

quiz.q: A student says 'centripetal force is a separate force that pushes objects outward in circular motion.' What is wrong with this statement?
o: Centripetal force points inward and is supplied by real forces like tension or gravity, not a separate outward force
Centripetal force always points outward, which is correct
Centripetal force is not a real physical effect
Centripetal force only applies to satellites
quiz.e: Centripetal force is simply the name for the net inward force in circular motion, provided by real forces (tension, gravity, friction, normal force) — it is not a distinct outward-pushing force.

quiz.q: At the bottom of a vertical circular loop, apparent weight (normal force) compared to true weight mg is:
quiz.e: At the bottom, N - mg = mv^2/r, so N = mg + mv^2/r, which is greater than mg.

quiz.q: A 60 kg pilot experiences 3g at the bottom of a vertical dive turn. What is the normal force the seat exerts on the pilot?
quiz.e: Apparent weight = 3mg = 3 x 60 x 9.8 = 1764 N.

quiz.q: Which statement about gravitational force between two masses is correct?
o: It acts along the line connecting the centers of the two masses
It only acts on the more massive object
It depends on the surface distance, not center-to-center distance
It is repulsive for like masses
quiz.e: Gravitational force is always attractive and acts along the line joining the centers of mass of the two objects.

quiz.q: An astronaut in a stable circular orbit feels 'weightless.' What is the best physical explanation?
o: The astronaut and spacecraft are both in free fall, accelerating together at the same rate due to gravity
There is no gravity in orbit
The astronaut has no mass in orbit
quiz.e: In orbit, gravity is the only force acting, providing centripetal acceleration. Since the astronaut and spacecraft accelerate together, there's no relative normal force between them, producing apparent weightlessness — gravity itself has not vanished.

quiz.q: A 0.20 kg object swings in a horizontal circle of radius 0.50 m on a string, completing one revolution every 2.0 s. What is the tension in the string?
If Earth's mass suddenly doubled but its radius stayed the same, the acceleration due to gravity at the surface would:
quiz.e: g = GM/r^2, so g is directly proportional to M. Doubling M doubles g when r is unchanged.

quiz.q: A 500 kg satellite orbits at a radius where orbital speed is 7000 m/s. What is the centripetal acceleration if r = 7.0 x 10^6 m?
Which of the following correctly ranks required centripetal force if speed is held constant but radius increases?
o: Required force decreases as radius increases
Required force increases as radius increases
Required force is independent of radius
quiz.e: F_c = mv^2/r. With v and m fixed, F_c is inversely proportional to r, so increasing r decreases the required centripetal force.

quiz.q: A moon orbits a planet in a perfect circle. Which pair of quantities remains constant throughout the orbit (assuming no other forces)?
quiz.e: In a stable circular orbit, both speed and the radius stay constant, even though the velocity vector (direction) and acceleration vector directions are constantly changing (though their magnitudes are also constant).

quiz.q: Which best explains why astronauts train using apparent weightlessness in a diving aircraft ('vomit comet')?
o: The aircraft is in free fall, so passengers and aircraft accelerate together under gravity alone, just like in orbit
The aircraft cancels gravity using engines
There is no air resistance at high altitude
The aircraft spins to create centrifugal force
quiz.e: During the dive, the aircraft's engines are cut so it free-falls under gravity alone, matching the acceleration of the passengers inside — the same effect as being in orbit.

quiz.q: For two satellites orbiting the same planet, the one at a larger radius has:
o: A slower orbital speed and a longer period
A faster orbital speed and a shorter period
The same orbital speed but a longer period
A faster orbital speed and a longer period
quiz.e: Both v = sqrt(GM/r) and T = 2*pi*sqrt(r^3/GM) show that increasing r decreases orbital speed and increases the period.

quiz.q: A 2.0 kg object is swung in a vertical circle of radius 1.5 m. At the bottom, its speed is 6.0 m/s. What is the tension in the string?
Why does a satellite not need fuel to maintain a stable circular orbit around Earth (ignoring atmospheric drag)?
o: Gravity alone provides exactly the centripetal force needed for the orbital speed and radius, requiring no additional thrust
Space has no gravity, so no force is needed
The satellite's engines fire continuously to balance gravity
Friction with the vacuum keeps it moving
quiz.e: In a stable orbit, gravity supplies exactly the required centripetal force for that speed and radius, so the satellite continues in uniform circular motion with no need for propulsion, per Newton's first law along the tangential direction.

quiz.q: An object moves in a circle of radius 2.0 m with a period of 4.0 s. What is its angular velocity?
quiz.e: omega = 2*pi/T = 2*pi/4.0 = 1.57 rad/s.

quiz.q: Which statement about the Moon's orbit around Earth is most accurate based on Kepler's laws?
o: The Moon moves faster when it is closer to Earth (perigee) than when farther away (apogee)
The Moon moves at constant speed throughout its orbit
The Moon moves slower when closer to Earth
The Moon's speed is unrelated to its distance from Earth
quiz.e: Kepler's Second Law (equal areas in equal times) implies the Moon sweeps through its orbit faster when nearer Earth (perigee) and slower when farther away (apogee), for its slightly elliptical orbit.

quiz.q: A 1500 kg car travels over the top of a hill shaped like a circular arc of radius 40 m at 15 m/s. What is the normal force from the road?
A satellite of mass m orbits at radius r with speed v around a planet of mass M. Which equation correctly expresses the force balance for the orbit?
quiz.e: Setting gravitational force equal to the required centripetal force: GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r, which simplifies to v = sqrt(GM/r).

quiz.q: A wheel starts from rest and reaches an angular velocity of 12 rad/s in 4.0 s. What is its angular acceleration?
quiz.e: alpha = Delta(omega)/Delta t = (12 - 0)/4.0 = 3.0 rad/s^2.

quiz.q: A disk rotates with angular velocity 5.0 rad/s at a radius of 0.20 m from the axis. What is the linear (tangential) speed at that radius?
quiz.e: v = omega x r = 5.0 x 0.20 = 1.0 m/s.

quiz.q: A force of 10 N is applied perpendicular to a wrench at a distance of 0.30 m from the bolt. What is the torque?
quiz.e: tau = rF sin(theta) = 0.30 x 10 x sin(90) = 3.0 N*m.

quiz.q: A force of 10 N is applied at 0.30 m from a pivot, but at an angle of 30 degrees to the lever arm (not perpendicular). What is the torque?
quiz.e: tau = rF sin(theta) = 0.30 x 10 x sin(30) = 3.0 x 0.5 = 1.5 N*m.

quiz.q: For maximum torque from a given force applied at a fixed distance from the pivot, the force should be applied:
o: At 45 degrees to the lever arm
In any direction; angle doesn't matter
quiz.e: tau = rF sin(theta) is maximized when sin(theta) = 1, i.e., theta = 90 degrees (force perpendicular to the lever arm).

quiz.q: What is the moment of inertia of a solid disk of mass 2.0 kg and radius 0.50 m about its central axis?
A thin hoop (ring) of mass 3.0 kg and radius 0.40 m rotates about its central axis. What is its moment of inertia?
Two objects have the same mass and radius: a solid disk and a hoop. Which has the greater moment of inertia about its central axis?
quiz.e: Hoop: I = MR^2. Disk: I = (1/2)MR^2. Since all the hoop's mass is at the rim (maximum distance from axis), the hoop has twice the disk's moment of inertia.

quiz.q: A net torque of 6.0 N*m is applied to a wheel with moment of inertia 2.0 kg*m^2. What is the angular acceleration?
quiz.e: alpha = tau/I = 6.0/2.0 = 3.0 rad/s^2, from Newton's second law for rotation, sum(tau) = I*alpha.

quiz.q: A rod of mass 4.0 kg and length 2.0 m rotates about an axis through its center, perpendicular to its length. What is its moment of inertia?
The same rod (4.0 kg, 2.0 m) instead rotates about an axis through one end. What is the new moment of inertia?
The parallel axis theorem states that I about a parallel axis a distance d from the center of mass axis is:
quiz.e: The parallel axis theorem: I = I_cm + Md^2, always increasing the moment of inertia compared to the center-of-mass axis.

quiz.q: A figure skater spinning with arms extended pulls her arms in close to her body. What happens to her angular velocity?
quiz.e: Pulling arms in decreases moment of inertia I. Since angular momentum L = Iw is conserved (no external torque), decreasing I means omega must increase.

quiz.q: What quantity is conserved in the figure skater example (previous question), assuming no external torque?
quiz.e: Angular momentum L = Iw is conserved when there is no external torque; kinetic energy actually increases as she pulls her arms in (she does work pulling them in).

quiz.q: A 1.0 kg point mass moves in a circle of radius 0.50 m with speed 4.0 m/s. What is its angular momentum about the center?
A merry-go-round with moment of inertia 300 kg*m^2 spins at 2.0 rad/s. What is its rotational kinetic energy?
A solid sphere and a hollow sphere of the same mass and radius are released from rest at the top of the same incline and roll without slipping. Which reaches the bottom first?
o: They arrive at the same time
quiz.e: The solid sphere has a smaller moment of inertia (2/5 MR^2 vs 2/3 MR^2 for the hollow sphere), so less of its energy goes into rotation and more into translation, giving it greater linear speed and a shorter time to the bottom.

quiz.q: An object rolls without slipping down an incline. What condition relates its center-of-mass speed v_cm to its angular speed omega?
quiz.e: The rolling-without-slipping condition is v_cm = omega x r (and a_cm = alpha x r), ensuring the contact point is instantaneously at rest relative to the surface.

quiz.q: What two conditions must both be satisfied for an extended object to be in complete static equilibrium?
quiz.e: Static equilibrium requires both translational equilibrium (sum F = 0) and rotational equilibrium (sum tau = 0 about any pivot point).

quiz.q: A uniform 5.0 m beam of weight 200 N is supported at both ends. A 100 N weight hangs 2.0 m from the left end. What is the torque of the hanging weight about the left support?
quiz.e: tau = rF = 2.0 m x 100 N = 200 N*m about the left support (force perpendicular to the beam).

quiz.q: When solving equilibrium problems, choosing the pivot point at the location of an unknown force is useful because:
o: It eliminates that unknown force from the torque equation since its lever arm is zero
It doubles the torque from that force
It is required by Newton's third law
quiz.e: Since torque = rF sin(theta), a force acting exactly at the pivot has r = 0, so its torque about that pivot is zero, removing it from the equation and simplifying the algebra.

quiz.q: Units of torque are most correctly stated as:
quiz.e: Torque has units of N*m. Although dimensionally the same as joules, torque is not energy, so N*m (not J) is used to avoid confusion, and it is a vector-like quantity (has sign/direction) unlike scalar energy.

quiz.q: A rotating flywheel has angular velocity that decreases from 20 rad/s to 5.0 rad/s over 5.0 s under a constant torque. What is the angular acceleration?
A wheel with moment of inertia 0.40 kg*m^2 starts from rest and undergoes angular acceleration of 2.5 rad/s^2 for 4.0 s. What angle (in radians) does it rotate through?
Which of the following best explains why a long wrench makes it easier to loosen a tight bolt than a short one, using the same applied force?
o: A longer lever arm (r) produces greater torque for the same force
A longer wrench weighs more, adding force
The bolt experiences less friction with a longer wrench
Torque is independent of the wrench's length
quiz.e: tau = rF sin(theta); increasing r (the length of the wrench, i.e., the lever arm) directly increases torque for the same applied force.

quiz.q: A solid sphere of mass 2.0 kg and radius 0.10 m has what moment of inertia about an axis through its center?
Angular momentum is best defined as:
o: The rotational analogue of linear momentum, L = I*omega
quiz.e: Angular momentum L = I*omega is the rotational counterpart to linear momentum p = mv, describing the 'quantity of rotation' an object has.

quiz.q: A net torque of 4.0 N*m acts on a rotating disk for 3.0 s. What is the resulting angular impulse (change in angular momentum)?
quiz.e: Angular impulse = tau x Delta t = 4.0 x 3.0 = 12 kg*m^2/s = Delta L.

quiz.q: A rolling ball has both translational and rotational kinetic energy. The total kinetic energy is correctly expressed as:
quiz.e: A rolling object's total KE is the sum of its translational KE (from center-of-mass motion) and rotational KE (from spinning about its center of mass).

quiz.q: A 2.0 kg solid disk of radius 0.30 m rolls without slipping down a hill, dropping a height of 1.0 m from rest. Using energy conservation with I = (1/2)MR^2, what is its speed at the bottom?
Why does a rolling object without slipping lose no mechanical energy to friction, even though static friction acts on it?
o: Static friction acts at the contact point which has zero instantaneous velocity, so it does no work
Static friction is always zero during rolling
There is no friction between the object and the surface
Kinetic friction replaces static friction and does no work
quiz.e: In rolling without slipping, the contact point is instantaneously at rest relative to the surface, so the static friction force there does zero work (W = F*d*cos(theta), but d = 0 for that point over an instant).

quiz.q: A 0.50 kg point mass is attached to a massless rod of length 0.80 m and rotates about the far end. What is the moment of inertia?
A student claims 'if the net force on an object is zero, the net torque must also be zero.' Is this correct?
o: No, an object can have zero net force but nonzero net torque (e.g., equal and opposite forces applied at different points)
Yes, zero net force always implies zero net torque
Yes, because force and torque are the same quantity
No, torque only exists when there is a net force
quiz.e: A couple (two equal, opposite, non-collinear forces) has zero net force but produces a nonzero net torque, showing the two equilibrium conditions are independent.

quiz.q: Which combination correctly matches a linear quantity to its rotational analogue?
o: Force <-> Torque, Mass <-> Moment of inertia, Momentum <-> Angular momentum
Force <-> Moment of inertia, Mass <-> Torque
quiz.e: The correct rotational analogues are: force -> torque, mass -> moment of inertia, linear momentum -> angular momentum, and linear velocity/acceleration -> angular velocity/acceleration.

quiz.q: A wheel of moment of inertia 5.0 kg*m^2 rotating at 10 rad/s is brought to rest by a constant torque over 2.0 s. What torque was applied?
Two disks with the same mass but different radii (disk A has twice the radius of disk B) rotate with the same angular velocity. Which has greater rotational kinetic energy?
o: Cannot be determined without more information
quiz.e: I = (1/2)MR^2 depends on R^2, so disk A (with twice the radius) has 4 times the moment of inertia, and thus 4 times the rotational KE at the same omega.

quiz.q: A gymnast performing a somersault tucks into a ball shape mid-air to spin faster. What principle explains this?
o: Conservation of angular momentum: decreasing moment of inertia increases angular velocity
Conservation of energy alone, without any momentum principle
quiz.e: Tucking reduces the gymnast's moment of inertia. Since no external torque acts on the free-falling body, angular momentum L = I*omega is conserved, so omega must increase.

quiz.q: A torque wrench applies 40 N*m to tighten a bolt with the wrench held at 0.25 m from the bolt, perpendicular to the handle. What force is being applied?
quiz.e: tau = rF, so F = tau/r = 40/0.25 = 160 N.

quiz.q: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, which statement is TRUE?
o: All points have the same angular velocity, but different linear speeds depending on their distance from the axis
All points have the same linear speed
All points have the same angular acceleration but different angular velocities
Points closer to the axis move faster than points farther away
quiz.e: In rigid body rotation, every point shares the same angular velocity omega, but linear speed v = omega*r increases with distance from the axis.

quiz.q: A constant net torque of 8.0 N*m acts on a wheel with moment of inertia 4.0 kg*m^2, starting from rest. What is the wheel's angular velocity after 3.0 s?
quiz.e: alpha = tau/I = 8.0/4.0 = 2.0 rad/s^2. omega = omega_0 + alpha*t = 0 + 2.0(3.0) = 6.0 rad/s.

quiz.q: A wave has a frequency of 5.0 Hz and a wavelength of 2.0 m. What is its speed?
quiz.e: v = f*lambda = 5.0 x 2.0 = 10 m/s.

quiz.q: A wave travels at 340 m/s with a wavelength of 0.85 m. What is its frequency?
A wave passes from air into water. Which property of the wave stays the same?
quiz.e: Frequency is determined by the source and does not change when a wave crosses into a new medium; wavelength and speed both change.

quiz.q: A string under tension 40 N has a linear mass density of 0.010 kg/m. What is the wave speed on the string?
If the tension in a string is quadrupled while linear mass density stays the same, the wave speed:
quiz.e: v = sqrt(F_T/mu), so v is proportional to sqrt(F_T). Quadrupling F_T increases v by a factor of sqrt(4) = 2.

quiz.q: Two waves meet such that a crest aligns with another crest. This is an example of:
quiz.e: When crests align with crests (waves in phase), the displacements add, producing a larger combined amplitude — constructive interference.

quiz.q: Two waves meet such that a crest aligns with a trough of equal amplitude. What results?
o: Complete destructive interference (cancellation at that point)
quiz.e: When a crest meets a trough of equal amplitude, the displacements are opposite and cancel, producing complete destructive interference at that instant/location.

quiz.q: Two speakers emit identical sound waves in phase. At a point where the path difference from the two speakers is exactly 2 wavelengths, what type of interference occurs?
quiz.e: A path difference of a whole number of wavelengths (nλ, here n=2) means the waves arrive in phase, producing constructive interference.

quiz.q: At a point where the path difference from two in-phase sources is 2.5 wavelengths, what type of interference occurs?
quiz.e: A path difference of (n + 1/2)*lambda (here n=2, giving 2.5*lambda) means the waves arrive out of phase, producing destructive interference.

quiz.q: A string fixed at both ends has length 2.0 m. What is the wavelength of its fundamental (first harmonic) standing wave?
quiz.e: For a string fixed at both ends, lambda_n = 2L/n. For the fundamental, n=1: lambda_1 = 2(2.0)/1 = 4.0 m.

quiz.q: A string of length 1.5 m fixed at both ends has wave speed 60 m/s. What is the fundamental frequency?
For the same string (L = 1.5 m, v = 60 m/s), what is the frequency of the third harmonic?
A pipe closed at one end has length 1.0 m. Which harmonics can it support?
quiz.e: A pipe closed at one end (open at the other) only supports odd harmonics because a node must exist at the closed end and an antinode at the open end.

quiz.q: A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental frequency of 100 Hz. What is the frequency of its next harmonic (third harmonic)?
quiz.e: For a closed-open pipe, only odd harmonics exist: f_n = n*f_1 for n=1,3,5,... The next harmonic after the fundamental (n=1) is n=3: f_3 = 3 x 100 = 300 Hz.

quiz.q: An organ pipe open at both ends has length 2.0 m and the speed of sound is 340 m/s. What is its fundamental frequency?
quiz.e: For an open-open pipe, f_1 = v/(2L) = 340/(2 x 2.0) = 340/4.0 = 85 Hz.

quiz.q: Two tuning forks with frequencies 440 Hz and 445 Hz are struck together. What beat frequency is heard?
quiz.e: Beat frequency = |f1 - f2| = |440 - 445| = 5 Hz.

quiz.q: An ambulance siren emits a fixed frequency. As the ambulance approaches a stationary listener, the listener hears a frequency that is:
quiz.e: This is the Doppler effect: when a source approaches an observer, the observed frequency increases (wavefronts are compressed in front of the moving source).

quiz.q: As the same ambulance moves away from the listener after passing, the listener hears a frequency that is:
quiz.e: As the source recedes, the observed frequency decreases because the wavefronts are stretched out behind the moving source.

quiz.q: A source emits sound at 500 Hz. If the source moves toward a stationary observer at 34 m/s (speed of sound = 340 m/s), what frequency does the observer hear?
What is the approximate speed of sound in air at room temperature?
quiz.e: The speed of sound in air at room temperature (~20 C) is approximately 343 m/s, much slower than the speed of light (3.0x10^8 m/s).

quiz.q: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum because:
o: Sound is a mechanical wave that requires a medium of particles to propagate
Sound travels too fast in a vacuum
Sound has no frequency in a vacuum
Sound waves are transverse and need a solid
quiz.e: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave that propagates via particle-to-particle collisions; without a medium, there is nothing to transmit the vibration.

quiz.q: The loudness of a sound is most directly associated with which wave property?
quiz.e: Loudness corresponds to the wave's amplitude/intensity, while pitch corresponds to frequency.

quiz.q: A sound source's intensity at 2.0 m is I. What is the intensity at 4.0 m from the source (assuming spherical spreading, inverse-square law)?
quiz.e: Intensity follows I proportional to 1/r^2. Doubling the distance (2.0 m to 4.0 m) reduces intensity by a factor of 2^2 = 4, so new intensity = I/4.

quiz.q: A sound has intensity 10^-6 W/m^2. Given I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2, what is its sound level in decibels?
What is a node in a standing wave?
o: A point of zero displacement that never moves
The point where the wave was generated
quiz.e: A node is a point of permanently zero displacement in a standing wave pattern, formed by destructive interference of the two traveling waves.

quiz.q: What is the distance between adjacent nodes in a standing wave?
quiz.e: Adjacent nodes (and adjacent antinodes) in a standing wave are separated by lambda/2.

quiz.q: A transverse wave reflects off a fixed (rigid) boundary. What happens to the reflected wave's phase?
quiz.e: A wave reflecting off a fixed/denser boundary undergoes a 180-degree phase inversion, while reflection off a free/less-dense boundary does not invert.

quiz.q: Which best describes diffraction of waves?
o: The bending/spreading of waves around obstacles or through openings
The change in wave speed when entering a new medium
The addition of two overlapping waves
The reflection of a wave off a boundary
quiz.e: Diffraction is the spreading of waves as they pass through an opening or around an obstacle, most noticeable when the opening/obstacle size is comparable to the wavelength.

quiz.q: A source of sound stays stationary while an observer moves toward it at speed v_o. How does this affect the observed frequency compared to when both are at rest?
o: The observed frequency is higher than the emitted frequency
The observed frequency is lower than the emitted frequency
The observed frequency equals the emitted frequency
The wave speed in air increases
quiz.e: When the observer moves toward a stationary source, they encounter wavefronts more frequently, resulting in f_obs = f_src(v+v_o)/v, which is higher than f_src.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of a longitudinal wave?
quiz.e: Sound is a longitudinal wave: the air molecules oscillate parallel to the direction the wave travels (compressions and rarefactions).

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of a transverse wave?
o: A wave on a plucked guitar string
A pressure wave in a gas
quiz.e: A wave on a string is transverse: the string oscillates perpendicular to the direction the wave travels along the string.

quiz.q: A wave's amplitude is doubled while its frequency stays the same. What happens to the wave's intensity?
quiz.e: Wave intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude. Doubling amplitude increases intensity by a factor of 2^2 = 4.

quiz.q: A string vibrates in its second harmonic (n=2) pattern while fixed at both ends. How many nodes (not counting endpoints beyond the fixed ends) does this standing wave pattern have, INCLUDING the two fixed ends?
quiz.e: For the nth harmonic on a string fixed at both ends, there are (n+1) nodes including the endpoints. For n=2, that's 3 nodes total (both ends plus one in the middle).

quiz.q: A wave's speed depends on properties of the medium it travels through. Which of these does NOT directly affect wave speed on a string?
o: Whether the string is stretched more or less
quiz.e: v = sqrt(F_T/mu) depends only on tension and linear mass density — not on the wave's own frequency or amplitude. Changing the medium changes speed; frequency does not.

quiz.q: When a wave's frequency stays fixed but it enters a medium where it travels slower, what happens to its wavelength?
quiz.e: Since v = f*lambda and f is fixed by the source, a decrease in v (slower medium) requires a proportional decrease in lambda.

quiz.q: A car horn at 400 Hz is heard by a stationary observer as the car recedes at 20 m/s (v_sound = 340 m/s). What frequency is heard?
Which statement correctly compares an open-open pipe and a closed-open pipe of the same length L?
o: The closed-open pipe has a lower fundamental frequency (only half as many wavelengths fit)
The open-open pipe has a lower fundamental frequency
The closed-open pipe supports more harmonics
quiz.e: Open-open: f_1 = v/(2L). Closed-open: f_1 = v/(4L), which is half the open-open fundamental — the closed-open pipe has a lower fundamental frequency and only odd harmonics.

quiz.q: A guitarist presses a string to shorten its vibrating length. What happens to the fundamental frequency?
quiz.e: f_1 = v/(2L), so decreasing the vibrating length L increases the fundamental frequency, producing a higher-pitched note.

quiz.q: What best describes 'beats' in sound?
o: A periodic rise and fall in loudness caused by interference of two close but different frequencies
A constant loud tone from constructive interference
The Doppler shift of a moving source
quiz.e: Beats arise from the superposition of two waves with slightly different frequencies, creating a periodic variation in amplitude (loudness) at the beat frequency |f1-f2|.

quiz.q: A wave on a string has amplitude 0.02 m and travels at 15 m/s with frequency 30 Hz. What is its wavelength?
quiz.e: lambda = v/f = 15/30 = 0.5 m.

quiz.q: Two point charges of +2.0 uC and +3.0 uC are separated by 0.50 m. What is the magnitude of the force between them? (k = 8.99x10^9 N*m^2/C^2)
If the distance between two charges is doubled, the Coulomb force between them becomes:
quiz.e: F = kq1q2/r^2, an inverse-square law. Doubling r reduces F by a factor of 2^2 = 4, so the new force is F/4.

quiz.q: Two charges of the same sign will:
o: Exert no force on each other
quiz.e: Like charges (both positive or both negative) repel; opposite charges attract.

quiz.q: What is the electric field magnitude at a distance of 0.20 m from a point charge of +5.0 uC? (k = 8.99x10^9 N*m^2/C^2)
A charge of +2.0 uC experiences a force of 0.040 N in an electric field. What is the field strength at that location?
Electric field lines around an isolated positive point charge:
o: Point radially outward, away from the charge
Point radially inward, toward the charge
quiz.e: Field lines emanate outward from positive charges (the direction a positive test charge would be pushed) and converge into negative charges.

quiz.q: Two electric field lines from different sources can:
o: Cross only if charges are equal
quiz.e: Field lines represent the net field direction at each point; since the field has only one direction at any point, field lines cannot cross.

quiz.q: A charge moves through a potential difference of 12 V. If the charge is 2.0 C, how much work is done on/by the charge?
In a uniform electric field of 500 N/C, what is the potential difference between two points separated by 0.10 m along the field direction?
quiz.e: For a uniform field, E = V/d, so V = Ed = 500 x 0.10 = 50 V.

quiz.q: A positive charge is released from rest in an electric field with no other forces. It will naturally move:
o: From high potential to low potential
From low potential to high potential
quiz.e: A positive charge moves in the direction of the electric field, which points from high to low potential (like a ball rolling downhill in potential energy).

quiz.q: What is the current in a wire if 6.0 C of charge passes a cross-section in 3.0 s?
quiz.e: I = Delta Q/Delta t = 6.0/3.0 = 2.0 A.

quiz.q: A resistor has a voltage of 12 V across it and a current of 3.0 A through it. What is its resistance?
quiz.e: R = V/I = 12/3.0 = 4.0 Ohm, from Ohm's Law V=IR.

quiz.q: A wire's length is doubled while its cross-sectional area and resistivity stay the same. What happens to its resistance?
quiz.e: R = rho*L/A, so resistance is directly proportional to length. Doubling L doubles R.

quiz.q: A wire's cross-sectional area is doubled while its length and resistivity stay the same. What happens to its resistance?
quiz.e: R = rho*L/A, so resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. Doubling A halves R.

quiz.q: What is the power dissipated by a resistor with R = 10 Ohm carrying a current of 2.0 A?
A 60 W light bulb operates at 120 V. What current does it draw?
Three resistors of 2.0 Ohm, 3.0 Ohm, and 5.0 Ohm are connected in series. What is the equivalent resistance?
quiz.e: In series, resistances add: R_eq = 2.0 + 3.0 + 5.0 = 10 Ohm.

quiz.q: The same three resistors (2.0, 3.0, 5.0 Ohm) are instead connected in parallel. Which statement about the equivalent resistance is true?
o: It is less than 2.0 Ohm (less than the smallest individual resistor)
It equals the average, about 3.3 Ohm
quiz.e: For parallel resistors, 1/R_eq = 1/2.0 + 1/3.0 + 1/5.0 = 0.5+0.333+0.2 = 1.033, so R_eq = 0.97 Ohm, which is less than the smallest individual resistor (2.0 Ohm) — always true for parallel combinations.

quiz.q: In a series circuit with a battery and several resistors, which quantity is the SAME through every resistor?
quiz.e: In a series circuit, there is only one path for current, so the same current flows through every element; voltage divides among the resistors.

quiz.q: In a parallel circuit, which quantity is the SAME across every branch?
quiz.e: In a parallel circuit, each branch is connected directly across the same two nodes, so the voltage across each branch is identical; current divides among the branches.

quiz.q: Two identical 4.0 Ohm resistors are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
quiz.e: 1/R_eq = 1/4.0 + 1/4.0 = 2/4.0 = 0.5, so R_eq = 2.0 Ohm. (For two identical resistors R in parallel, R_eq = R/2.)

quiz.q: A circuit has a 12 V battery connected to a single 6.0 Ohm resistor. What current flows and what power is dissipated?
Kirchhoff's Junction Rule is a statement of which conservation law?
quiz.e: The junction rule (total current in = total current out at any junction) is a direct consequence of conservation of electric charge.

quiz.q: Kirchhoff's Loop Rule is a statement of which conservation law?
quiz.e: The loop rule (sum of voltage changes around a closed loop = 0) reflects conservation of energy, since potential is a measure of energy per charge.

quiz.q: A battery has EMF 9.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ohm. When it delivers a current of 2.0 A, what is its terminal voltage?
quiz.e: Terminal voltage V = EMF - I*r = 9.0 - 2.0(0.50) = 9.0 - 1.0 = 8.0 V.

quiz.q: An ammeter used to measure current in a circuit branch should be connected:
o: In series with that branch, and should have very low resistance
In parallel with that branch, and should have very low resistance
In series, and should have very high resistance
In parallel, and should have very high resistance
quiz.e: An ammeter must be placed in series to measure the current actually flowing through the branch, and should have negligible resistance so it doesn't alter the circuit's current.

quiz.q: A voltmeter used to measure voltage across a resistor should be connected:
o: In parallel with the resistor, and should have very high resistance
In series with the resistor, and should have very high resistance
In parallel, and should have very low resistance
In series, and should have very low resistance
quiz.e: A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the component being measured and should have very high resistance so it draws negligible current, avoiding disturbance of the circuit.

quiz.q: Charge is best described as:
o: Quantized in units of e = 1.6x10^-19 C and conserved in a closed system
quiz.e: Electric charge comes in discrete multiples of the elementary charge e = 1.6x10^-19 C, and total charge is conserved in any isolated system.

quiz.q: A conductor differs from an insulator in that a conductor:
o: Allows charges to move freely through it
quiz.e: Conductors have free (mobile) charge carriers, typically electrons, that can move easily through the material, unlike insulators where charges are tightly bound.

quiz.q: What does it mean for two points to be on the same equipotential surface?
o: No work is required to move a charge between them along that surface
The electric field is strongest there
quiz.e: Points on the same equipotential surface have the same electric potential, so moving a charge between them (along the surface) requires zero work, since W=qDeltaV=0.

quiz.q: Equipotential surfaces are always oriented ___ relative to electric field lines.
quiz.e: Electric field lines are always perpendicular to equipotential surfaces, pointing in the direction of decreasing potential.

quiz.q: A 100 Ohm resistor and a 25 Ohm resistor are connected in series to a 10 V battery. What is the current in the circuit?
For the circuit in the previous question (100 Ohm and 25 Ohm resistors in series with 10 V), what is the voltage drop across the 25 Ohm resistor?
quiz.e: Current is the same through both series resistors: I = 0.08 A. V_25 = IR = 0.08 x 25 = 2.0 V.

quiz.q: A 6.0 Ohm and a 3.0 Ohm resistor are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. What is the total current supplied by the battery?
Why does adding another resistor in parallel to an existing parallel combination always decrease the equivalent resistance?
o: It provides an additional path for current to flow, increasing total conductance
It increases the total length of wire
It increases the total resistivity of the circuit
Parallel resistors always add directly like series resistors
quiz.e: Adding a parallel branch adds another path for current, increasing total conductance (1/R_eq), which always decreases the equivalent resistance, regardless of the new resistor's value.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly compares gravitational force and Coulomb's electric force?
o: Both follow an inverse-square law with distance, but gravity is always attractive while Coulomb's force can be attractive or repulsive
Both can be attractive or repulsive
Gravity follows an inverse-square law but Coulomb's force does not
Coulomb's force is always attractive like gravity
quiz.e: F_g = Gm1m2/r^2 and F_E = kq1q2/r^2 share the same inverse-square mathematical form, but gravity is only attractive (masses are always positive) while Coulomb's force can be attractive (opposite charges) or repulsive (like charges).

quiz.q: A charge of -4.0 uC is placed in a uniform electric field pointing to the right with magnitude 2000 N/C. What is the direction of the force on the charge?
o: To the right (same as the field)
quiz.e: Force on a charge is F=qE. Since the charge is negative, the force points opposite to the field direction, i.e., to the left.

quiz.q: Resistivity of most metals generally does what as temperature increases?
o: Increases, due to more frequent electron collisions
quiz.e: As temperature rises, atoms vibrate more, causing more frequent collisions with charge carriers, which increases resistivity (and thus resistance) in most metals.

quiz.q: A 12 V battery is connected to two resistors in series: 4.0 Ohm and 8.0 Ohm. What is the voltage drop across the 8.0 Ohm resistor?
Why is charging by induction different from charging by direct contact?
o: Induction separates charge on a nearby object without any direct transfer of charge between objects
Induction requires physical contact between the objects
Induction destroys charge rather than redistributing it
quiz.e: Charging by induction uses the electric field of a nearby charged object to redistribute (polarize) charge on a second object, without any charge actually transferring between them via contact.

quiz.q: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration?
An object's position-time graph is a straight line with negative slope. What does this indicate?
quiz.e: A straight line on an x-t graph has constant slope, i.e., constant velocity; negative slope means constant negative velocity.

quiz.q: A ball is thrown straight up with initial speed 15 m/s. How long until it returns to its starting height? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
quiz.e: Total flight time t = 2v₀/g = 2(15)/9.8 ≈ 3.06 s.

quiz.q: Which quantity is a scalar rather than a vector?
quiz.e: Distance has magnitude only (no direction), unlike displacement, velocity, and acceleration.

quiz.q: A projectile is launched horizontally from a cliff at 20 m/s. If it lands 2 s later, how far does it travel horizontally?
quiz.e: Horizontal velocity is constant: x = v₀t = 20(2) = 40 m.

quiz.q: On a velocity-time graph, what does the area under the curve represent?
quiz.e: Area under a v-t graph equals the displacement (integral of velocity over time).

quiz.q: A car moving at 30 m/s brakes with acceleration −6 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping?
Two objects are dropped from the same height at the same time, one twice as massive as the other. Ignoring air resistance, which hits the ground first?
o: They land at the same time
quiz.e: In free fall, acceleration due to gravity is independent of mass, so both hit simultaneously.

quiz.q: A particle's velocity is given by v(t) = 4t. What is its acceleration at t = 3 s?
quiz.e: a = dv/dt = 4 m/s², constant regardless of time.

quiz.q: An object thrown at an angle of 45° above horizontal has the maximum range compared to other angles (same speed, level ground) because:
quiz.e: Range R = v₀²sin(2θ)/g is maximized when sin(2θ)=1, i.e., θ=45°.
