quiz.q: A ball rolls off a table with horizontal velocity 3 m/s and lands 0.5 s later. What is its vertical velocity just before landing?
quiz.e: v_y = gt = 9.8(0.5) = 4.9 m/s downward.

quiz.q: Which pair of graphs correctly relate for constant nonzero acceleration?
o: x-t is linear, v-t is linear
x-t is parabolic, v-t is linear
x-t is linear, v-t is parabolic
x-t is parabolic, v-t is parabolic
quiz.e: With constant acceleration, x(t) is quadratic (parabola) and v(t) is linear.

quiz.q: A runner covers 100 m in 10 s but the track is a closed loop returning to start. What is the runner's displacement?
quiz.e: Displacement depends only on start and end position; returning to start gives zero displacement despite nonzero distance.

quiz.q: A car accelerates from 10 m/s to 25 m/s over 100 m. What is its acceleration?
During the rise of a projectile, which statement about vertical acceleration is true?
o: It is zero at the peak
It is constant and equal to −g throughout
It changes sign only at launch
quiz.e: Gravity acts continuously; vertical acceleration is −g at every point of the trajectory, including the peak.

quiz.q: A stone is dropped from rest and falls for 3 s. How far does it fall? (g=9.8 m/s²)
A vector has components vₓ=3 m/s and v_y=4 m/s. What is its magnitude?
quiz.e: Magnitude = √(3²+4²) = √25 = 5 m/s.

quiz.q: An object moving in the +x direction experiences a constant acceleration in the −x direction. What is happening to the object's speed?
quiz.e: Acceleration opposite velocity decelerates the object; it will slow, stop, then reverse direction and speed up backward.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four constant-acceleration kinematic equations?
quiz.e: F=ma is Newton's second law, not a kinematics equation.

quiz.q: A projectile has the same launch and landing height. Doubling its initial speed (same angle) changes the range by a factor of:
quiz.e: Range ∝ v₀², so doubling v₀ quadruples the range.

quiz.q: A car travels at constant 20 m/s for 5 s, then decelerates at 4 m/s² to rest. Total distance traveled?
quiz.e: First leg: 20×5=100 m. Deceleration distance: v²=v₀²+2aΔx→0=400−8Δx→Δx=50 m. Total=150 m.

quiz.q: What does a negative slope on an acceleration-time graph physically represent?
quiz.e: The slope of an a-t graph is the rate of change of acceleration (jerk); negative slope means acceleration is decreasing.

quiz.q: An arrow is shot at 30° above horizontal at 40 m/s. What is its initial vertical velocity component?
Two cars start at the same point; Car A moves at constant 10 m/s, Car B starts from rest with a=2 m/s². When do they have the same velocity?
A ball is thrown upward and caught at the same height it was released. Which statement is true about its velocity at launch and at catch?
quiz.e: By symmetry of projectile motion, the speed is the same at equal heights but direction reverses (up vs down).

quiz.q: A car's velocity-time graph shows a straight line from (0,10) to (4,10) then a line dropping to (8,0). Total displacement over 8 s?
quiz.e: First segment: 10×4=40 m (rectangle). Second: ½×10×4=20 m (triangle). Total=60 m.

quiz.q: What is the horizontal range formula for a projectile launched and landing at the same height?
quiz.e: Standard projectile range formula for equal launch/landing elevation is R = v₀²sin(2θ)/g.

quiz.q: An object has zero velocity but nonzero acceleration. Which scenario fits?
o: A ball at the peak of its vertical throw
A car parked with engine off
An object moving at constant speed
A ball resting on the ground
quiz.e: At the peak of vertical motion, v=0 momentarily but gravity still gives a=−g.

quiz.q: A student mistakenly uses Δx = v₀t instead of Δx = v₀t + ½at² for accelerating motion. This error would:
o: Have no effect on the result
quiz.e: Ignoring the ½at² term removes the extra distance gained from acceleration, underestimating displacement when a>0.

quiz.q: A rock is thrown horizontally from a 20 m tall cliff. How long does it take to hit the ground? (g=9.8 m/s²)
Which of the following best describes average speed vs average velocity for a round trip?
o: Average speed > average velocity in general
quiz.e: For a round trip, displacement (hence average velocity magnitude) is less than or equal to distance (hence average speed), and often strictly less.

quiz.q: A ball is dropped and its velocity after 2 s is 19.6 m/s. What was its initial velocity?
quiz.e: v=v₀+gt → 19.6=v₀+9.8(2) → v₀=19.6−19.6=0, consistent with being 'dropped.'

quiz.q: If air resistance is included in projectile motion, which of the following changes from the idealized case?
o: Horizontal velocity is no longer constant
Vertical acceleration becomes greater than g
Time is no longer a shared variable
quiz.e: Air resistance introduces a horizontal drag force, so horizontal velocity is no longer constant as it is in the idealized (no-drag) model.

quiz.q: A car travels 60 m in the first 3 s of uniform acceleration from rest. What is its acceleration?
When solving 2D projectile problems, why can horizontal and vertical motions be treated independently?
o: Gravity has no horizontal component and there is no horizontal acceleration force
Time runs differently in each direction
Horizontal and vertical velocities are always equal
Only vertical motion follows kinematics equations
quiz.e: Since gravity acts only vertically, the horizontal and vertical components of motion are independent, connected only through shared time.

quiz.q: A ball thrown at 20 m/s at 60° above horizontal. What is the vertical velocity component?
quiz.e: v_y0 = v₀sinθ = 20 sin60° ≈ 17.3 m/s.

quiz.q: An object undergoes constant negative acceleration while moving in the positive direction. Its speed-time graph will show:
o: A straight line decreasing to zero then increasing (as speed) after reversing
A straight line increasing the whole time
quiz.e: Speed decreases to zero as velocity approaches zero, then as the object reverses, speed increases again — giving a V-shaped speed graph even though velocity itself is linear.

quiz.q: Which statement about instantaneous velocity is correct?
o: It equals the slope of the tangent line to the x-t curve at that instant
It cannot be zero if acceleration is nonzero
quiz.e: Instantaneous velocity is defined as the slope of the tangent to the position-time graph at a given instant.

quiz.q: A ball is launched at 25 m/s at 37° (sin37°≈0.6, cos37°≈0.8). What is the max height reached? (g=9.8)
A person walks 3 m east then 4 m north. What is the magnitude of their total displacement?
quiz.e: Pythagorean theorem: √(3²+4²)=5 m.

quiz.q: A 5 kg object experiences a net force of 15 N. What is its acceleration?
According to Newton's Third Law, if a hammer strikes a nail with 200 N, the nail exerts on the hammer:
o: 0 N since the nail doesn't move
quiz.e: Newton's Third Law requires equal magnitude, opposite direction force on the hammer from the nail.

quiz.q: A book rests on a table. Which pair of forces are Newton's Third Law partners?
o: Book's weight and the table pushing up on the book
Book pushing down on table and table pushing up on book
Book's weight and normal force on book
Table's weight and normal force from floor
quiz.e: Third law pairs act on different objects: book-on-table and table-on-book, both the same type of (normal) force.

quiz.q: A 10 kg crate is pulled by a horizontal force of 40 N; friction opposes with 10 N. What is the acceleration?
quiz.e: Net force = 40−10=30 N; a=F/m=30/10=3 m/s².

quiz.q: An elevator accelerates upward at 2 m/s². A 60 kg person's apparent weight is:
A block sits on a frictionless 30° incline. What is its acceleration down the slope? (g=9.8)
A box remains stationary on a rough surface even though a 20 N horizontal force is applied. What can be concluded?
quiz.e: Since the box is in equilibrium, static friction must balance the applied force, so f_s=20 N.

quiz.q: Two blocks (2 kg and 3 kg) are connected by a string over a frictionless pulley, with the 3 kg block hanging. What is the system's acceleration? (g=9.8)
quiz.e: a = (m2 g)/(m1+m2) = (3×9.8)/5 = 5.88 m/s² (assuming 2 kg on frictionless horizontal surface, 3 kg hanging).

quiz.q: Which statement correctly describes inertia?
o: The tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion
A force that pushes objects to rest
The force of gravity on an object
The rate of change of momentum
quiz.e: Inertia is the resistance to changes in velocity, quantified by mass.

quiz.q: A 1000 kg car experiences a braking force of 4000 N. What is its deceleration?
The coefficient of kinetic friction between a 5 kg block and the floor is 0.2. What is the kinetic friction force? (g=9.8)
An astronaut in deep space (negligible gravity) pushes off a space station. Why does she accelerate away?
o: Newton's Third Law: the station pushes back on her with equal, opposite force
She has no inertia in space
quiz.e: Her push on the station is met by an equal and opposite reaction force from the station on her, accelerating her (F=ma with her much smaller mass).

quiz.q: A 2 kg object is in free fall near Earth's surface. What is the net force acting on it? (g=9.8)
quiz.e: Net force = weight = mg = 2(9.8)=19.6 N, since air resistance is neglected.

quiz.q: A block on a 20° frictionless incline has mass 4 kg. What is the normal force? (g=9.8)
Which of the following is an example of a Newton's First Law scenario?
o: A hockey puck sliding at constant velocity on frictionless ice
A car accelerating from a stoplight
quiz.e: Constant velocity with zero net force (frictionless ice) exemplifies Newton's First Law (inertia).

quiz.q: A person pushes a wall with 100 N but the wall does not move. According to Newton's Third Law, the wall pushes back with:
quiz.e: Reaction force is always equal in magnitude and opposite in direction: 100 N on the person.

quiz.q: A 3 kg block is pushed with a 20 N force up a frictionless incline at angle 25° along the slope. What is its acceleration up the incline? (g=9.8, sin25°≈0.4226)
Two forces act on an object: 6 N east and 8 N north. What is the magnitude of the net force?
quiz.e: Perpendicular forces combine via Pythagorean theorem: √(6²+8²)=10 N.

quiz.q: A 50 kg skier accelerates down a 15° slope with kinetic friction coefficient 0.1. What is the net acceleration? (g=9.8)
When a rocket expels gas downward to launch upward, this is best explained by:
quiz.e: The rocket exerts force on the exhaust gas; the gas exerts an equal, opposite force back on the rocket, propelling it upward.

quiz.q: A 4 kg block hangs from two symmetric strings, each making 30° with the vertical ceiling attachment. What is the tension in each string? (g=9.8)
quiz.e: Vertical equilibrium: 2T cos30° = mg → T = mg/(2cos30°) = 39.2/1.732 ≈ 22.6 N.

quiz.q: Which best describes static equilibrium?
o: The net force and net torque on an object are both zero
The object has zero velocity only
The object experiences only one force
quiz.e: Static equilibrium requires ΣF=0 and Στ=0, meaning no linear or rotational acceleration.

quiz.q: A 2 kg cart on a frictionless track is pulled by two horizontal ropes: one 10 N right, one 4 N left. Find the acceleration.
quiz.e: Net force = 10−4=6 N right; a=6/2=3 m/s².

quiz.q: On the Moon (g≈1.6 m/s²), how does an object's mass compare to its weight relative to Earth?
o: Mass is unchanged, weight is less
Mass is less, weight is unchanged
Both mass and weight are unchanged
Both mass and weight decrease equally
quiz.e: Mass is an intrinsic property (unchanged), while weight = mg depends on local gravitational field strength, which is smaller on the Moon.

quiz.q: A 6 kg box is at rest on a surface with μ_s=0.4. What is the maximum static friction force before it starts sliding? (g=9.8)
A person stands on a scale in an elevator accelerating downward at 3 m/s². If their mass is 70 kg, what does the scale read? (g=9.8)
Which statement about tension in an ideal (massless) string over a frictionless pulley is correct?
o: Tension is the same throughout the string
Tension depends on the pulley's mass
Tension is zero if the string is taut
quiz.e: For an ideal massless string and frictionless, massless pulley, tension is uniform throughout the string.

quiz.q: A 1500 kg car takes a turn while maintaining constant speed on a flat road. Is there a net force acting on it?
o: Yes, directed toward the center of the turn
Yes, directed away from the center
No, since it's Newton's First Law
quiz.e: Even at constant speed, changing direction requires centripetal (net) force directed toward the center of the curve.

quiz.q: An object of mass m is pushed with force F at angle θ above horizontal across a surface with friction coefficient μ. Which term reduces the normal force?
o: The vertical component of the applied force, F sinθ
The horizontal component of the applied force
quiz.e: When pushing at an upward angle, N = mg − F sinθ, since the vertical component of the push partially supports the object's weight.

quiz.q: A 12 N force and an 8 N force act in opposite directions on a 4 kg object. What is its acceleration?
quiz.e: Net force=12−8=4 N; a=4/4=1 m/s².

quiz.q: Why does a heavier object not accelerate faster than a lighter one in free fall, despite experiencing greater gravitational force?
o: Greater weight is exactly offset by greater inertia (mass) in F=ma
Air resistance always cancels the difference
Heavier objects have less gravity acting on them
This is only true on the Moon
quiz.e: F=mg and a=F/m=g; the mass cancels out, so acceleration is independent of mass despite larger force on more massive objects.

quiz.q: A block is being pulled at constant velocity across a rough floor by a horizontal rope. What must be true about the forces?
o: Applied force equals friction force, and normal force equals weight
Applied force is greater than friction
quiz.e: Constant velocity means zero net force, so applied force = friction and normal force = weight (no vertical acceleration).

quiz.q: A spring scale reads the tension in a string holding a stationary 2 kg mass. What does it read? (g=9.8)
quiz.e: For a stationary hanging mass, tension equals weight: T=mg=2(9.8)=19.6 N.

quiz.q: In a tug-of-war where neither side moves, what can be said about the net force on the rope?
o: Zero, since the rope is in equilibrium
Equal to the winning team's pull
Equal to the losing team's pull
quiz.e: If the rope (and system) isn't accelerating, the net force on it is zero, meaning both teams pull with equal magnitude forces.

quiz.q: A 3000 kg truck decelerates from 20 m/s to rest in 5 s. What average force does this require?
Which best explains why pushing a heavy box is harder to start moving than to keep moving?
o: Static friction coefficient is typically greater than kinetic friction coefficient
Kinetic friction always exceeds static friction
quiz.e: μ_s is generally greater than or equal to μ_k, so more force is needed to overcome static friction and initiate motion than to sustain it.

quiz.q: A 5 kg block on a horizontal frictionless surface is connected by a string over a pulley to a hanging 5 kg block. What is the acceleration of the system? (g=9.8)
A crate is in equilibrium on an incline due to friction. Which relationship must hold?
o: f_s = mg sinθ (static friction balances the gravity component along the incline)
quiz.e: For equilibrium on an incline (no applied force besides gravity and friction), static friction must equal the component of gravity along the slope, mg sinθ.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a fundamental assumption typically made about an 'ideal' pulley in AP Physics 1 problems?
o: It has significant mass and rotational inertia
It redirects tension without changing its magnitude
The string over it is massless
quiz.e: Ideal pulleys are typically assumed massless and frictionless in AP Physics 1, not with significant mass/inertia.

quiz.q: A net force of 0 N acts on a moving object. What happens to its velocity?
quiz.e: By Newton's First Law, zero net force means zero acceleration, so velocity stays constant.

quiz.q: A 2 kg object moves at 5 m/s. What is its momentum?
A 0.5 kg ball experiences a net force of 20 N for 0.1 s. What is the impulse delivered?
Two skaters, initially at rest, push off each other. Skater A (50 kg) moves at 2 m/s. If skater B has mass 40 kg, what is B's speed?
quiz.e: Momentum conservation: 0=m_A v_A − m_B v_B (opposite directions) → 50(2)=40(v_B) → v_B=2.5 m/s.

quiz.q: A 1000 kg car moving at 15 m/s collides with a stationary 1000 kg car and they lock together. What is their common velocity after collision?
quiz.e: Perfectly inelastic: m1v1=(m1+m2)v_f → 1000(15)=2000(v_f) → v_f=7.5 m/s.

quiz.q: Which quantity is always conserved in a collision within an isolated system, regardless of collision type?
quiz.e: Momentum is conserved in all collisions in an isolated system; kinetic energy is only conserved in elastic collisions.

quiz.q: A ball with momentum 6 kg·m/s bounces off a wall and returns with momentum −4 kg·m/s (opposite direction). What is the impulse delivered by the wall?
quiz.e: Impulse = Δp = p_f − p_i = −4 − 6 = −10 kg·m/s.

quiz.q: Why do airbags reduce injury during a car crash?
o: They increase the time over which momentum changes, reducing the average force
They increase the force needed to stop a passenger
They reduce the passenger's momentum change
quiz.e: By extending Δt for the same Δp (impulse), airbags reduce the average force experienced by the passenger (F=Δp/Δt).

quiz.q: A 3 kg object moving at 4 m/s collides elastically with a stationary 3 kg object. What are their velocities after collision (equal masses, elastic, head-on)?
o: First object stops, second moves at 4 m/s
First continues at 4 m/s, second stays at rest
quiz.e: For an elastic collision between equal masses with one initially at rest, velocities exchange completely: the moving object stops and the stationary one takes on its velocity.

quiz.q: A 2 kg cart moving at 3 m/s and a 4 kg cart moving at -1 m/s (opposite direction) collide and stick together. What is their final velocity?
A rifle of mass 4 kg fires a 0.02 kg bullet at 300 m/s. What is the rifle's recoil speed?
quiz.e: Momentum conservation: 0 = m_bullet v_bullet + m_rifle v_rifle → v_rifle = -(0.02×300)/4 = -1.5 m/s (magnitude 1.5 m/s).

quiz.q: Which of these best defines impulse?
o: The change in momentum of an object, equal to net force times time interval
The total momentum of a system
The force acting on an object at one instant
The change in kinetic energy of an object
quiz.e: Impulse J = FΔt = Δp, the change in momentum caused by a net force applied over a time interval.

quiz.q: In a perfectly inelastic collision between two objects, what happens to kinetic energy?
o: Some kinetic energy is converted to other forms (heat, sound, deformation)
Momentum is lost instead of kinetic energy
quiz.e: Perfectly inelastic collisions conserve momentum but not kinetic energy; the objects sticking together dissipates some KE as heat/sound/deformation.

quiz.q: A 60 kg astronaut at rest in space throws a 2 kg tool at 10 m/s away from the space station. What is the astronaut's resulting speed?
quiz.e: Momentum conservation: 0 = m_tool v_tool + m_astronaut v_astronaut → v_astronaut = -(2×10)/60 ≈ -0.33 m/s (opposite direction).

quiz.q: Two objects have equal momentum but different masses. Which has greater kinetic energy?
o: Cannot be determined without more information
quiz.e: KE = p²/(2m); for equal p, smaller mass gives larger KE since KE is inversely proportional to mass at fixed momentum.

quiz.q: A force-time graph shows a triangular pulse peaking at 100 N over 0.2 s. What is the impulse delivered?
quiz.e: Impulse = area under F-t graph = ½ × base × height = ½(0.2)(100) = 10 N·s.

quiz.q: During an explosion of a stationary object into two fragments, what is true about the total momentum immediately after?
o: It equals zero, matching the initial momentum
It equals the sum of the individual fragment kinetic energies
It is undefined since it's an explosion
It increases due to the explosion's energy
quiz.e: Momentum conservation requires total momentum after (vector sum of fragments) to equal the initial momentum, which was zero for a stationary object.

quiz.q: A 5 kg block moving at 4 m/s hits a wall and stops in 0.02 s. What average force does the wall exert on the block?
For a system's center of mass to remain at constant velocity, what condition must be met?
o: No net external force acts on the system
All objects must have equal mass
The system must be at rest
quiz.e: Internal forces (collisions, explosions) do not affect the center of mass motion; only a net external force changes it.

quiz.q: A 1 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides elastically with a stationary 2 kg ball. Using momentum and KE conservation, what is the 1 kg ball's velocity after? (elastic 1D formula: v1' = ((m1-m2)/(m1+m2))v1)
Which scenario best demonstrates the impulse-momentum theorem in real life?
o: A catcher moving their glove backward while catching a fast ball to reduce force
A ball resting on a table
A car moving at constant velocity on a highway
A book sitting still on a shelf
quiz.e: Moving the glove back increases the time (Δt) over which the ball's momentum changes, reducing the force felt by the catcher, per J=FΔt=Δp.

quiz.q: Two ice skaters push off from rest. Skater A (mass 80 kg) ends up moving at 1.5 m/s. What is the total momentum of the system after they push off?
quiz.e: Since they start at rest (zero total momentum) and momentum is conserved with no external horizontal force, the total momentum remains zero after pushing off.

quiz.q: A 1500 kg car traveling at 20 m/s crashes into a barrier and stops in 0.5 s. What average force does the barrier exert?
In a 2D collision between two pucks on ice, which quantities must be separately conserved?
o: The x-component and y-component of total momentum
quiz.e: In 2D, momentum conservation applies independently to each perpendicular component (x and y).

quiz.q: A 0.15 kg baseball approaches a bat at 40 m/s and leaves at -50 m/s (reversed direction) after being hit. If contact lasts 0.001 s, what average force does the bat exert?
Which of the following is true about a perfectly elastic collision?
o: Both total momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved
Neither momentum nor kinetic energy is conserved
quiz.e: By definition, an elastic collision conserves both total momentum and total kinetic energy.

quiz.q: A 2000 kg truck moving at 10 m/s rear-ends a stationary 1000 kg car, and they don't stick (elastic assumption not required, just find combined system momentum). What is the total momentum right after impact (system, before any separation)?
quiz.e: Total momentum is conserved from before collision: p=m_truck v_truck=2000(10)=20,000 kg·m/s (stationary car contributes 0).

quiz.q: A tennis ball bounces off a racket. Which factor increases the impulse delivered to the ball for a given change in the racket's force profile?
o: A longer contact time between racket and ball
quiz.e: Impulse = FΔt; for a similar average force, a longer contact time increases the total impulse (and thus momentum change) delivered.

quiz.q: A 4 kg object at rest explodes into two 2 kg pieces. One piece moves at 5 m/s east. What is the velocity of the other piece?
quiz.e: Momentum conservation: 0=2(5)+2(v) → v=-5 m/s, i.e., 5 m/s west.

quiz.q: Which best explains why momentum, not kinetic energy, is the quantity always conserved in collisions?
o: Momentum conservation follows from Newton's Third Law regardless of the type of internal forces during collision
Kinetic energy is not a real physical quantity
Kinetic energy only applies to elastic collisions by definition and cannot be tracked otherwise
quiz.e: Since collision forces are internal action-reaction pairs (Newton's Third Law), they cancel in the total system momentum calculation regardless of how much KE is dissipated.

quiz.q: A 5 kg cart moving right at 2 m/s collides with an 8 kg cart moving left at 3 m/s. If they stick together, what is the final velocity (taking right as positive)?
A ball of mass 0.4 kg is dropped and hits the ground at 8 m/s, bouncing back up at 6 m/s. What is the magnitude of the impulse from the ground?
quiz.e: Taking down as positive: p_i=0.4(8)=3.2, p_f=0.4(-6)=-2.4; Δp=-2.4-3.2=-5.6, magnitude 5.6 kg·m/s.

quiz.q: During a collision, if the contact time is doubled while impulse stays the same, what happens to the average force?
quiz.e: Since J=FΔt is fixed, doubling Δt requires F to be halved to keep the product (impulse) constant.

quiz.q: A system of two colliding carts has total momentum 20 kg·m/s before collision. What is the total momentum immediately after, assuming no external horizontal forces?
o: Depends on whether it's elastic or inelastic
quiz.e: Momentum is conserved regardless of collision type (elastic or inelastic) as long as the system is isolated from external forces.

quiz.q: A 0.06 kg tennis ball is served at 50 m/s. Contact time with the racket is 0.005 s. What average force did the racket exert (starting from rest)?
Which of these best describes a 'glancing' (2D) collision analysis approach?
o: Decompose velocities into x and y components and conserve momentum in each direction independently
Ignore angles and use 1D formulas directly
Only consider the heavier object's momentum
quiz.e: 2D collisions require resolving all velocities into perpendicular components and applying momentum conservation separately along each axis.

quiz.q: A 1200 kg car and a 1200 kg car of identical mass collide head-on at equal speeds (20 m/s each, opposite directions) and stick together. What is their velocity after collision?
quiz.e: Total momentum=1200(20)+1200(-20)=0, so combined velocity after is 0 m/s (they stop).

quiz.q: How does a longer follow-through in a golf swing (increasing contact time with the ball) affect the force needed to achieve a given ball speed?
o: It reduces the average force needed for the same impulse
It increases the average force needed
It has no effect on force since impulse is fixed by ball mass alone
It converts impulse into pure kinetic energy directly
quiz.e: Since J=FΔt=Δp is fixed by the desired change in the ball's momentum, a longer contact time (Δt) allows a smaller average force (F) to produce the same impulse.

quiz.q: A 10 N force pushes a box 5 m in the direction of the force. How much work is done?
quiz.e: W=Fd cosθ=10(5)cos0°=50 J.

quiz.q: A person carries a bag horizontally at constant height across a room. How much work does gravity do on the bag?
quiz.e: Gravity is vertical, displacement is horizontal, so the angle is 90° and cosθ=0, giving zero work.

quiz.q: A 2 kg object speeds up from 3 m/s to 6 m/s. What is the change in kinetic energy?
A spring with k=200 N/m is compressed 0.1 m. What is the elastic potential energy stored?
A 5 kg ball is dropped from 10 m. Ignoring air resistance, what is its speed just before hitting the ground? (g=9.8)
A machine does 500 J of work in 10 s. What is its power output?
A block slides down a frictionless ramp from rest and reaches the bottom with KE=100 J. If friction were present and did −20 J of work, what would the final KE be?
quiz.e: With friction, some mechanical energy converts to heat: final KE = 100 − 20 = 80 J.

quiz.q: According to the work-energy theorem, the net work done on an object equals:
quiz.e: W_net = ΔKE is the statement of the work-energy theorem.

quiz.q: A 1000 kg car increases speed from 10 m/s to 20 m/s. How much work was done on it?
A pendulum swings from its highest point (v=0) to its lowest point. Which energy transformation occurs (ignoring air resistance)?
o: Gravitational PE converts entirely to KE
quiz.e: At the highest point all energy is gravitational PE; at the lowest point (reference height) all of it has converted to KE, conserving total mechanical energy.

quiz.q: A crane lifts a 200 kg object 15 m at constant velocity. How much work does the crane do? (g=9.8)
quiz.e: At constant velocity, applied force = weight = mg = 1960 N; W=Fd=1960×15=29,400 J.

quiz.q: A car engine delivers 60 kW while the car moves at 20 m/s. What is the driving force? (assume force parallel to velocity)
Which of the following is a conservative force?
o: Applied pushing force with varying direction
quiz.e: Gravity does path-independent work, making it conservative; friction is non-conservative because it depends on path length.

quiz.q: A ball is thrown upward with KE=40 J. Ignoring air resistance, what is its KE at the top of its trajectory (vertical throw)?
quiz.e: At the peak of a purely vertical throw, velocity is zero, so KE=0 (all energy converted to gravitational PE).

quiz.q: A spring is stretched from x=0 to x=0.2 m with k=150 N/m. How much work is done to stretch it?
A 0.5 kg cart moving at 4 m/s collides with a wall and stops. How much kinetic energy was lost?
quiz.e: KE_i=½(0.5)(16)=4 J; KE_f=0, so 4 J is lost (converted to heat/sound/deformation).

quiz.q: Which statement about power is correct?
o: Power is the rate of doing work, P=W/t
Power is the same as work when time is 1 hour
Power and energy have the same units
Power depends only on force, not time
quiz.e: Power measures how quickly work is done or energy transferred: P=W/t=ΔE/t.

quiz.q: A roller coaster car at height 20 m has speed 5 m/s. It descends to height 5 m. Ignoring friction, what is its speed there? (g=9.8)
quiz.e: Energy conservation: ½v_i²+gh_i=½v_f²+gh_f → v_f=√(v_i²+2g(h_i−h_f))=√(25+2(9.8)(15))=√(25+294)=√319≈17.9 m/s.

quiz.q: A box is pushed 10 m by a 30 N force applied at 60° above the direction of motion. How much work is done?
If the net work done on an object over some interval is zero, what can be concluded?
quiz.e: By the work-energy theorem, zero net work means zero change in kinetic energy, though the object could still have moved (with balanced forces) or changed direction.

quiz.q: A 3 kg block slides across a rough floor with friction coefficient 0.25, traveling 4 m. How much energy is dissipated as heat? (g=9.8)
quiz.e: Friction force=μmg=0.25(3)(9.8)=7.35 N; heat=f×d=7.35×4=29.4 J.

quiz.q: Two objects, one twice the mass of the other, move at the same speed. How do their kinetic energies compare?
o: The heavier one has twice the kinetic energy
The heavier one has four times the kinetic energy
The lighter one has more kinetic energy
quiz.e: KE=½mv²; with equal v, KE is proportional to mass, so double mass means double KE.

quiz.q: A 60 kg hiker climbs to the top of a hill 200 m high in 30 minutes. What is the hiker's average power output? (g=9.8)
A block on a frictionless surface is attached to a spring, oscillating back and forth. At maximum compression, what is true?
o: KE is minimum (zero) and spring PE is maximum
KE is maximum and spring PE is zero
Both KE and PE are zero
Total energy is at its lowest
quiz.e: At maximum compression, the block momentarily stops (KE=0), and all mechanical energy is stored as spring potential energy.

quiz.q: A person does 200 J of work lifting a box, but the box's PE only increases by 150 J. Where did the other 50 J likely go?
o: Kinetic energy of the box and/or heat from friction/inefficiency
It is stored as normal force
quiz.e: Energy is conserved; the remaining 50 J likely went into kinetic energy of the box or was lost to friction/heat, not destroyed.

quiz.q: A 1500 W motor lifts a load at constant speed of 0.5 m/s. What is the maximum weight it can lift?
In an ideal (frictionless) pendulum, mechanical energy is conserved. What happens to KE and PE as the pendulum swings from the bottom to the side?
o: KE decreases, PE increases, sum constant
quiz.e: As height increases (swinging outward), PE increases and KE decreases correspondingly, keeping total mechanical energy constant.

quiz.q: A car's brakes convert kinetic energy into what form of energy primarily?
quiz.e: Friction in the brakes converts the car's kinetic energy mostly into heat (thermal energy).

quiz.q: A 2 kg object falls from rest and has fallen 3 m. What is its kinetic energy at that point (ignoring air resistance)? (g=9.8)
quiz.e: KE=mgh=2(9.8)(3)=58.8 J (energy conservation, since PE lost = KE gained).

quiz.q: A spring-loaded launcher (k=500 N/m) is compressed 0.05 m and launches a 0.1 kg ball. What is the ball's launch speed (assume all spring energy converts to KE)?
Which quantity is NOT conserved in an inelastic collision?
quiz.e: Inelastic collisions conserve momentum and total energy but not kinetic energy, some of which converts to heat, sound, or deformation.

quiz.q: A worker pushes a cart with a 50 N force over 8 m; friction does −400 J of work over that distance. If the cart starts and ends at rest, what is the net work done on the cart?
quiz.e: Starts and ends at rest means ΔKE=0, so by the work-energy theorem net work must be 0 J (applied work of 400 J is exactly canceled by friction's −400 J).

quiz.q: A 4 kg block starts at rest at the top of a frictionless 5 m tall ramp. What is its speed at the bottom? (g=9.8)
How does doubling an object's speed affect the work needed to stop it (via friction)?
quiz.e: KE∝v², so doubling speed quadruples KE, requiring four times the (negative) work to bring it to rest.

quiz.q: A 70 kg runner accelerates from 2 m/s to 8 m/s. How much work was done on the runner?
A weightlifter holds a barbell stationary above their head for 10 seconds. How much work is done on the barbell during this time?
o: Zero, since there is no displacement
Negative, since gravity acts on it
Depends on the barbell's mass only
quiz.e: Work requires displacement; since the barbell doesn't move, W=Fd=0 regardless of the force required to hold it.

quiz.q: A 0.2 kg ball is launched vertically and reaches a max height of 5 m. What was its initial kinetic energy (ignoring air resistance)? (g=9.8)
Which best describes the relationship between conservative forces and potential energy?
o: Potential energy can only be defined for conservative forces
All forces have an associated potential energy
Potential energy applies to friction as well
quiz.e: Potential energy is defined only for conservative forces (like gravity and springs) because their work is path-independent.

quiz.q: A 100 W bulb runs for 2 hours. How much energy does it consume?
A 4 kg block is pushed 6 m across a frictionless floor by a horizontal 8 N force, starting from rest. What is its final speed?
A 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s east collides head-on elastically with an identical stationary 2 kg ball. What happens to the velocities (equal mass elastic collision)?
o: The velocities are exchanged: the first stops, the second moves at 3 m/s east
quiz.e: For an elastic collision between equal masses with one at rest, the moving object transfers all its velocity to the stationary one.

quiz.q: A 0.02 kg dart moving at 100 m/s embeds in a stationary 2 kg block on a frictionless surface. What is the resulting speed of block+dart?
quiz.e: Perfectly inelastic: v_f = m_dart v_dart/(m_dart+m_block) = (0.02×100)/2.02 ≈ 0.99 m/s.

quiz.q: A soccer ball of mass 0.45 kg is kicked, changing its velocity from 0 to 20 m/s in 0.01 s. What average force did the foot exert?

T^2 is proportional to r^3 for all objects orbiting the same central body.

On a frictionless banked curve, a component of the normal force provides centripetal force: tan(theta) = v^2/(rg).
tau = rF*sin(theta), the rotational analogue of force; measures how effectively a force causes angular acceleration about a pivot.
I = sum(m*r^2); the rotational analogue of mass, depending on both mass and its distribution relative to the rotation axis.

KE_rot = (1/2)*I*omega^2, the kinetic energy stored in a rotating object.
v_cm = omega*r and a_cm = alpha*r; static friction (not kinetic) allows rolling without energy loss.

flashcards.d: I = (1/2)*M*R^2 about its central axis.
A spinning skater pulling arms inward decreases I, so omega increases to keep L = I*omega constant.
An object is in static equilibrium only if BOTH the net force is zero AND the net torque about any pivot is zero.
v = f*lambda, relating wave speed, frequency, and wavelength; frequency is set by the source and does not change across media.
v = sqrt(F_T/mu), where F_T is string tension and mu is linear mass density (mass per length).
Occurs when waves meet in phase (path difference = n*lambda), producing a larger combined amplitude.
Occurs when waves meet out of phase (path difference = (n+1/2)*lambda), reducing or canceling amplitude.

flashcards.d: Harmonic frequencies f_n = n*v/(2L) for n = 1, 2, 3,...; supports all integer harmonics.

flashcards.d: Only odd harmonics exist: f_n = n*v/(4L) for n = 1, 3, 5,...

f_beat = |f1 - f2|, the periodic loudness variation heard when two waves of close but different frequencies interfere.
Approximately 343 m/s at room temperature; sound is a longitudinal wave requiring a medium to travel.
beta = 10*log10(I/I0), where I0 = 10^-12 W/m^2 is the threshold of human hearing.

E = F/q = k*Q/r^2 (from a point charge), the force per unit positive test charge; units N/C.
V = U/q, measured in volts (J/C); potential difference (voltage) drives current flow between two points.
V = IR, relating voltage, current, and resistance for ohmic materials.
R = rho*L/A, increasing with length and resistivity, decreasing with cross-sectional area.
P = IV = I^2*R = V^2/R, the rate of electrical energy transfer or dissipation.
Resistors in series share the same current; R_eq = R1 + R2 + ...; voltage divides among them.
Resistors in parallel share the same voltage; 1/R_eq = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...; current divides among them.
The total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving it (conservation of charge).
The sum of voltage changes around any closed circuit loop equals zero (conservation of energy).
The vector change in position, Δx = x_f − x_i; depends only on initial and final points, not the path taken.
The slope of the tangent line to a position-time graph at a specific instant; the derivative of position with respect to time.
The rate of change of velocity with respect to time, a = Δv/Δt, measured in m/s².
Relates final velocity to initial velocity, constant acceleration, and time; used when displacement is not needed.
Gives displacement in terms of initial velocity, constant acceleration, and time.
Motion under gravity alone, with constant downward acceleration g = 9.8 m/s², independent of the object's mass.
Two-dimensional motion with constant horizontal velocity and constant vertical acceleration (−g), analyzed by treating each axis independently.
R = v₀²sin(2θ)/g for equal launch and landing heights; maximized at a launch angle of 45°.
A graph where the slope at any point equals the instantaneous velocity; a parabolic shape indicates constant acceleration.
A graph where the slope equals acceleration and the area under the curve equals displacement.
An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity, unless acted on by a net external force.
ΣF = ma; the net force on an object equals the product of its mass and acceleration, with acceleration in the direction of net force.
For every action force one object exerts on another, the second object exerts an equal and opposite force back on the first.
The perpendicular contact force a surface exerts on an object, preventing it from passing through the surface; not always equal to weight.
The force resisting the start of sliding between surfaces in contact, with maximum value f_s(max) = μ_s N.
The force opposing relative sliding motion between two surfaces, given by f_k = μ_k N, generally less than max static friction.
The pulling force transmitted through a string, rope, or cable; uniform throughout an ideal massless string over a frictionless pulley.
A diagram showing all external forces acting on a single object as vectors, used to apply Newton's Second Law systematically.
The normal force experienced by an object, which differs from true weight (mg) when the object has vertical acceleration, such as in an elevator.
Gravity on an incline splits into components mg sinθ (along the slope) and mg cosθ (perpendicular to the slope, balanced by normal force).
The product of an object's mass and velocity, p = mv; a vector quantity measured in kg·m/s.
The change in momentum caused by a net force acting over a time interval: J = FΔt = Δp.
In an isolated system with no net external force, total momentum before an event equals total momentum after.
A collision in which both total momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved.
A collision in which momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not; some energy converts to heat, sound, or deformation.
A collision where the colliding objects stick together and move with a common final velocity: m1v1+m2v2=(m1+m2)v_f.
States that the impulse delivered to an object equals its change in momentum, connecting force-time behavior to velocity change.
The mass-weighted average position of a system, which moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a net external force, unaffected by internal collisions or explosions.
The backward momentum of an object (e.g., a gun) that results from conservation of momentum when it propels another object (e.g., a bullet) forward.
A graph whose area under the curve equals the impulse delivered to an object during that time interval.
The energy transferred by a force acting through a displacement: W = Fd cosθ, measured in joules.
The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ΔKE.
The energy of motion, KE = ½mv²; proportional to mass and to the square of speed.
Stored energy due to height in a gravitational field, U_g = mgh, measured relative to a chosen reference level.
Energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring, U_s = ½kx², where k is the spring constant and x the displacement from equilibrium.
In the absence of non-conservative forces, KE + PE remains constant throughout a system's motion.
The rate of doing work or transferring energy, P = W/t = Fv cosθ, measured in watts (J/s).
A force (like gravity or spring force) whose work done is path-independent, allowing a potential energy to be defined.
The restoring force of an ideal spring: F = −kx, proportional and opposite to the displacement from equilibrium.
A force like friction whose work depends on the path taken, converting mechanical energy into other forms such as heat.

PART_A.q: What is the key distinction between distance and displacement?
o: Displacement is a vector giving straight-line change in position; distance is the scalar total path length traveled
Distance is a vector; displacement is a scalar
Both are always zero for a round trip
PART_A.e: Displacement depends only on initial and final position (a vector), while distance is the total length of the path traveled (a scalar) and can never decrease during motion, unlike displacement which can be zero even after significant motion (e.g., a round trip).

PART_A.q: According to Newton's second law, if the net force on an object doubles while its mass stays constant, what happens to its acceleration?
PART_A.e: a = F_net/m, so acceleration is directly proportional to net force at constant mass; doubling F doubles a.

PART_A.q: A net force does 40 J of work on a 5 kg object initially at rest. What is the object's final speed?
PART_A.e: Work-energy theorem: W_net = delta_KE = 1/2 m v^2 - 0. v = sqrt(2W/m) = sqrt(2(40)/5) = sqrt(16) = 4 m/s.

PART_A.q: A 2 kg cart moving at 3 m/s collides and sticks to a stationary 1 kg cart. What is their common velocity after the collision?
PART_A.e: Conservation of momentum: m1*v1 = (m1+m2)*v_f -> (2)(3) = (3)v_f -> v_f = 2 m/s.

PART_A.q: Which expression correctly gives the net centripetal force required to keep an object of mass m moving in a circle of radius r at constant speed v?
PART_A.e: Centripetal force follows from a_c = v^2/r and F = ma, giving F_c = mv^2/r, directed toward the center of the circle.

PART_A.q: A force of 20 N is applied perpendicular to a wrench at a distance of 0.5 m from the bolt. What is the magnitude of the torque produced?
PART_A.e: torque = r*F*sin(theta) = (0.5)(20)(sin 90 deg) = 10 N*m.

PART_A.q: A sound wave has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.68 m. What is its speed?
PART_A.e: v = f*lambda = (500 Hz)(0.68 m) = 340 m/s, consistent with the speed of sound in air.

PART_A.q: Two point charges of 2x10^-6 C each are separated by 0.3 m. Using k = 9x10^9 N*m^2/C^2, what is the magnitude of the electric force between them?
A ball is dropped from rest from a height of 45 m. Using g = 10 m/s^2 and ignoring air resistance, how long does it take to hit the ground?
A 10 kg box slides on a horizontal floor with a coefficient of kinetic friction of 0.2. Using g = 10 m/s^2, what is the magnitude of the kinetic friction force?
A pendulum bob is released from rest at a height of 0.8 m above its lowest point. Ignoring air resistance, and using g = 10 m/s^2, what is its speed at the lowest point?
PART_A.e: By conservation of mechanical energy, mgh = 1/2 m v^2, so v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2(10)(0.8)) = sqrt(16) = 4 m/s.

PART_A.q: A 5 kg object experiences a net force of 50 N for 0.2 s. What is the resulting change in its velocity?
PART_A.e: Impulse J = F*delta_t = (50)(0.2) = 10 N-s = delta_p = m*delta_v, so delta_v = 10/5 = 2 m/s.

PART_A.q: An object moves in a circle of radius 5 m at a constant speed of 10 m/s. What is its centripetal acceleration?
A 2 kg point mass is located 0.3 m from an axis of rotation. What is its moment of inertia about that axis?
A string of length 1 m, fixed at both ends, vibrates in its fundamental mode. If the wave speed on the string is 20 m/s, what is the fundamental frequency?
PART_A.e: For the fundamental mode on a string fixed at both ends, lambda1 = 2L = 2(1) = 2 m. f = v/lambda = 20/2 = 10 Hz.

PART_A.q: A resistor with resistance 4 ohms has a voltage of 12 V across it. What current flows through it?
PART_A.e: By Ohm's law, I = V/R = 12 V / 4 ohms = 3 A.

PART_A.q: On a velocity-vs-time graph, what physical quantity is represented by the area under the curve?
PART_A.e: The area under a v-t graph equals the integral of v dt over that interval, which is the displacement.

PART_A.q: Two blocks connected by a massless string hang over a frictionless pulley (Atwood machine). Which statement about the tension in the string is correct, assuming the blocks have different masses?
o: Tension is the same throughout the ideal string and less than the weight of the heavier block
Tension equals the weight of the heavier block
Tension equals the weight of the lighter block
Tension is zero because the system accelerates
PART_A.e: For a massless, inextensible string over an ideal pulley, tension is uniform throughout. Since the system accelerates, T must be less than the heavier block's weight and greater than the lighter block's weight.

PART_A.q: A motor does 500 J of work in 10 seconds. What is its average power output?
Which statement correctly distinguishes an elastic collision from an inelastic collision?
o: In an elastic collision, both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved; in an inelastic collision, only momentum is conserved
In an elastic collision, only kinetic energy is conserved
Momentum is conserved only in elastic collisions
Neither momentum nor energy is conserved in any collision
PART_A.e: Momentum is conserved in all collisions of an isolated system. Kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions; in inelastic collisions some KE converts to other forms (heat, sound, deformation).

PART_A.q: Two point masses of 5 kg and 3 kg are separated by 1 m. Using G = 6.67x10^-11 N*m^2/kg^2, what is the gravitational force between them (approximately)?
A figure skater spinning with arms extended pulls her arms in close to her body. Assuming no external torques, what happens to her angular velocity and why?
o: It increases, because decreasing moment of inertia must increase angular velocity to conserve angular momentum
It decreases, because pulling arms in decreases her mass
It stays the same, because angular momentum is unrelated to body shape
It increases because her kinetic energy is conserved
PART_A.e: Angular momentum L = I*omega is conserved with no external torque. Pulling her arms in reduces I, so omega must increase to keep L constant.

PART_A.q: A police siren emits a constant frequency. As the police car approaches a stationary observer, how does the sound the observer hears compare to the siren's actual frequency?
o: The observed frequency is higher than the emitted frequency
The observed frequency is lower than the emitted frequency
The observed frequency equals the emitted frequency
PART_A.e: By the Doppler effect, when a source moves toward a stationary observer, successive wavefronts are compressed, increasing the observed frequency (and shortening the observed wavelength) above the source's emitted frequency.

PART_A.q: Two identical resistors are first connected in series, then in parallel, across the same battery. Compared to the series combination, the parallel combination has:
o: Higher equivalent resistance and higher total current from the battery
Lower equivalent resistance and higher total current from the battery
Lower equivalent resistance and lower total current from the battery
The same equivalent resistance as series
PART_A.e: For two identical resistors R, series gives R_eq = 2R while parallel gives R_eq = R/2, which is lower. Since I = V/R_eq for a fixed battery voltage, the lower resistance in parallel yields higher total current drawn from the battery.

PART_A.q: A projectile is launched at 45 degrees above the horizontal with an initial speed of 20 m/s. Using g = 10 m/s^2, what is its horizontal range?
A person pushes on a wall with 50 N of force. By Newton's third law, what force does the wall exert on the person?
PART_A.e: Newton's third law: the wall exerts a reaction force equal in magnitude (50 N) and opposite in direction to the force the person applies.

PART_A.q: A spring with spring constant k = 200 N/m is compressed 0.5 m from equilibrium. How much elastic potential energy is stored?

A 3 kg ball moving at 4 m/s collides head-on with a stationary 1 kg ball. After the collision, the 3 kg ball moves at 2 m/s in the same direction. What is the velocity of the 1 kg ball after the collision?
PART_A.e: Conservation of momentum: m1*v1i = m1*v1f + m2*v2f -> (3)(4) = (3)(2) + (1)v2f -> 12 = 6 + v2f -> v2f = 6 m/s.

PART_A.q: According to Kepler's third law, how does a planet's orbital period T relate to its orbital radius r (for circular orbits)?
PART_A.e: Kepler's third law: T^2 is proportional to r^3, which follows from setting gravitational force equal to the required centripetal force for a circular orbit.

PART_A.q: A rotating object has a moment of inertia of 4 kg*m^2 and an angular velocity of 3 rad/s. What is its rotational kinetic energy?

PART_B1.q: A 4 kg object accelerates at 3 m/s^2 under a single applied horizontal force, while a 2 N friction force opposes its motion. What is the magnitude of the applied force?
PART_B1.e: Net force needed: F_net = m*a = 4(3) = 12 N. Since friction opposes motion, F_applied = F_net + f = 12 + 2 = 14 N.

PART_B1.q: A satellite orbits Earth in a circular orbit where gravity provides the centripetal force. Which equation correctly gives the satellite's orbital speed v in terms of G, Earth's mass M, and orbital radius r?
PART_B1.e: Setting gravitational force equal to centripetal force: GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r. Solving for v gives v = sqrt(GM/r).

PART_B1.q: Two resistors, 3 ohm and 6 ohm, are connected in series with a 9 V battery. What is the current through the circuit?
PART_B1.e: R_eq (series) = 3 + 6 = 9 ohm. I = V/R_eq = 9/9 = 1 A.

PART_B1.q: A 20 N force is applied at 60 degrees above a horizontal surface to drag a box 5 m horizontally. How much work does the force do?
A 300 N child sits 2 m from the pivot of a balanced seesaw. How far from the pivot must a 200 N child sit on the other side to balance it?
PART_B1.e: For rotational equilibrium, torques balance: (300)(2) = (200)(d) -> d = 600/200 = 3 m.

PART_B1.q: A car increases its velocity uniformly from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 4 s. What is its acceleration?
A 60 kg astronaut at rest in space throws a 2 kg tool at 10 m/s away from her. What is the magnitude of her resulting recoil speed?
PART_B1.e: Momentum conservation: 0 = m_tool*v_tool - m_astro*v_astro -> v_astro = (2)(10)/60 = 0.33 m/s, in the direction opposite the tool.

PART_B1.q: A wave has a period of 0.02 s. What is its frequency?
A block rests on a frictionless incline at angle theta. Which expression gives the component of gravitational acceleration accelerating the block down the incline?
PART_B1.e: On a frictionless incline, the component of gravitational acceleration along the incline surface is g*sin(theta); the perpendicular component g*cos(theta) is balanced by the normal force.

PART_B1.q: A 1000 kg car rounds a flat curve of radius 50 m at a constant speed of 20 m/s. What minimum coefficient of static friction is required to prevent sliding? (g = 10 m/s^2)
PART_B1.e: Required centripetal force: F_c = m*v^2/r = (1000)(400)/50 = 8000 N. This must be supplied by friction: mu*m*g = 8000 -> mu = 8000/(1000*10) = 0.8.

PART_B1.q: Two resistors, 4 ohm and 4 ohm, are connected in parallel. What is their equivalent resistance?
PART_B1.e: For resistors in parallel: 1/R_eq = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2, so R_eq = 2 ohm.

PART_B1.q: A 2 kg block slides down a frictionless ramp from a height of 5 m, then travels across a rough horizontal surface (mu_k = 0.3) before stopping. Using g = 10 m/s^2, how far does it slide across the rough surface before stopping?
PART_B1.e: Energy at the bottom of the ramp: KE = m*g*h = (2)(10)(5) = 100 J. Friction force f = mu_k*m*g = (0.3)(2)(10) = 6 N. Distance d = KE/f = 100/6 ~ 16.7 m.

PART_B1.q: A disk with moment of inertia 2 kg*m^2 spins at 5 rad/s. What is its angular momentum?
A cyclist starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s^2 for 6 s. What total distance does the cyclist cover?
A 0.5 kg ball hits a wall at 8 m/s and rebounds at 6 m/s in the opposite direction. What is the magnitude of the impulse delivered to the ball by the wall?
PART_B1.e: Taking the initial direction as positive: delta_p = m(v_f - v_i) = 0.5(-6 - 8) = 0.5(-14) = -7 N*s. The magnitude of the impulse is 7 N*s.

PART_B1.q: Two speakers emit sound waves of the same frequency and amplitude, in phase. At a point where the path difference from the two speakers equals one full wavelength, what type of interference occurs?
o: The waves cancel amplitude but not energy
PART_B1.e: A path difference equal to a whole number of wavelengths (here, 1 wavelength) means the waves arrive in phase, producing constructive interference and a louder sound.

PART_B1.q: Two blocks, 2 kg and 3 kg, are connected by a string and pulled across a frictionless surface by a 10 N horizontal force applied to the 3 kg block. What is the acceleration of the system?
PART_B1.e: Treating both blocks as one system, a = F_net/(m1+m2) = 10/(2+3) = 2 m/s^2.

PART_B1.q: An object's weight on the surface of a planet is W. At a height above the surface equal to the planet's radius (i.e., twice the distance from the center), how does the gravitational force on the object compare to W?
PART_B1.e: Gravitational force follows an inverse-square law, F is proportional to 1/r^2. Doubling the distance from the center reduces the force to 1/(2^2) = 1/4 of its original value, so the new weight is W/4.

PART_B1.q: How does the electric field strength from a point charge change if the distance from the charge is tripled?
PART_B1.e: Electric field from a point charge follows an inverse-square law, E is proportional to 1/r^2. Tripling the distance reduces the field to 1/(3^2) = 1/9 of its original strength.

PART_B1.q: A car engine delivers a constant driving force of 2000 N while the car travels at a constant 15 m/s. What is the engine's power output?

PART_B2.q: A 1500 kg car traveling at 20 m/s brakes and comes to rest over a distance of 50 m due to friction. What is the magnitude of the average friction force?
PART_B2.e: Using the work-energy theorem: friction does negative work equal to the car's initial KE. KE = 1/2*m*v^2 = 0.5(1500)(20)^2 = 300,000 J. F = W/d = 300,000/50 = 6000 N.

PART_B2.q: A capacitor-free circuit has a 6 ohm resistor in parallel with a 3 ohm resistor, and this combination is in series with a 2 ohm resistor, all connected to a 12 V battery. What is the total current supplied by the battery?
PART_B2.e: Parallel section: 1/R_p = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2, so R_p = 2 ohm. Total R = R_p + 2 = 2 + 2 = 4 ohm. I = V/R = 12/4 = 3 A.

PART_B2.q: A 0.2 kg ball on a 1.5 m string moves in a horizontal circle, completing one revolution every 2 seconds. What is the tension in the string (providing the centripetal force)? (use pi^2 ~ 9.87)
A 5 kg block on a rough horizontal surface (mu_k = 0.25) is pulled by a horizontal 40 N force. Using g = 10 m/s^2, what is the block's acceleration?
PART_B2.e: Friction force f = mu_k*m*g = 0.25(5)(10) = 12.5 N. Net force = 40 - 12.5 = 27.5 N. a = F_net/m = 27.5/5 = 5.5 m/s^2.

PART_B2.q: A guitar string of length 0.65 m produces a fundamental frequency of 330 Hz. What is the speed of the wave on the string?
PART_B2.e: For the fundamental mode, wavelength = 2L = 2(0.65) = 1.3 m. v = f*lambda = (330)(1.3) = 429 m/s.

PART_B2.q: A 1200 kg car moving at 15 m/s collides with a stationary 800 kg car, and the two vehicles lock together. Using conservation of momentum, what is their common velocity immediately after the collision?
PART_B2.e: Conservation of momentum: m1*v1 = (m1+m2)*v_f -> (1200)(15) = (2000)*v_f -> v_f = 18000/2000 = 9 m/s.

PART_B2.q: A ball thrown straight up returns to its starting height after 4 s of flight. Using g = 10 m/s^2, what was its initial speed?
PART_B2.e: Total flight time up and down is symmetric, so time to reach the top is 2 s. At the top, v = 0 = v0 - g*t_up -> v0 = g*t_up = (10)(2) = 20 m/s.

PART_B2.q: A solid disk (I = 1/2*m*r^2) of mass 4 kg and radius 0.5 m rolls without slipping. If its linear speed is 2 m/s, what is its total kinetic energy (translational + rotational)?
PART_B2.e: Translational KE = 1/2*m*v^2 = 0.5(4)(2)^2 = 8 J. Angular speed omega = v/r = 2/0.5 = 4 rad/s. I = 1/2*m*r^2 = 0.5(4)(0.25) = 0.5 kg*m^2. Rotational KE = 1/2*I*omega^2 = 0.5(0.5)(16) = 4 J. Total KE = 8 + 4 = 12 J.

PART_B2.q: A roller coaster car of mass 400 kg starts from rest at the top of a 20 m hill (frictionless) and descends to the bottom. Using g = 10 m/s^2, what is its kinetic energy at the bottom?
PART_B2.e: By conservation of energy, KE_bottom = m*g*h = (400)(10)(20) = 80,000 J.

PART_B2.q: Two charges, +4 microC and -2 microC, are placed 0.2 m apart. Using k = 9x10^9 N*m^2/C^2, what is the magnitude of the force between them, and is it attractive or repulsive?
PART_B2.e: F = k*|q1*q2|/r^2 = (9x10^9)(4x10^-6)(2x10^-6)/(0.2)^2 = (9x10^9)(8x10^-12)/0.04 = 0.072/0.04 = 1.8 N. Since the charges have opposite signs, the force is attractive.
